speechtext:
Mr. LaRIVIERE asked :
1.	Has the following memorial and supplement to the same, from the Manitoba and North-west Accounting Postmasters' Association been considered by the Honourable the Postmaster General ?
* Winnipeg, Man., February, 1903.
To the Right Hon. Sir. William Mulock, Postmaster General, Ottawa.
Dear Sir,-We, the undersigned, accounting postmasters of Manitoba, beg to bring to your attention the following statement of facts regarding our work, which goes to show that the remuneration is most inadequate, in the hope that you may be able to grant us substantial and immediate relief. We do this the more hopefully in view' of the stand you have taken on the question of hours of labour, &c., of the workingman.	1

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
1. The postmaster is responsible for the safe handling of many important letters and valuable parcels. In this country large amounts of money, formerly sent by express, are now sent by registered mail to wheat-buyers to enable them to carry on their business. In many places the branch banks remit to, or receive from, the head office large sums of money. This increases the postmaster's responsibility, and where help- is employed, necessitates care in the selection. The money-order business necessitates the handling of large sums of money for the miserable pittance of 26 cents per $100. The amount of stamps kept on hand must always be large with the source of supply so far away. In no other line of work would persons be held responsible for the proper handling of such large amounts, with the same possibilities of irregularities and losses, without remuneration at least from five to ten times greater than the postmaster receives for his money-order work. In many cases there is added responsibility through the handling of customs parcels, for which there is practically no remuneration. The postmaster is expected to provide a roomy, centrally located office without any regard to the rental which that office would command if leased for other purposes. The necessity for the correct aud prompt despatch of all mails, regardless of hours of arrival and departure, is in many instances a very grave responsability. Understanding that the present basis of remuneration has been in vogue for a quarter of a century or more, we would respectfully point out various increases in work which clearly show that, although it may have been sufficient then, it is utterly inadequate now.
Firstly.-In connection with newspapers and periodicals, we think it is a conservative estimate to assume that a family will now receive an average of six or eight times as many periodicals as a family would be receiving twenty-five or thirty years ago.
Secondly.-The use of the mails a,s a means of distributing advertising matter is a practice of recent years entirely, and- the quantity handled is simply enormous and constantly increasing. These increases affect both local distribution and the sorting of matter for forwarding to outside offices.
Thirdly.-The recent reduction in the rate of letter postage necessitates (in the matter of Canadian and United States postage) an increase of fully fifty per cent in the number of letters handled before an increase of revenue can accrue, or an increase of salary be hoped for. In the case of British, an<j some other lines of foreign postage, the increase in the number of letters must be 150 per cent before we have established a basis for any possible increase in salary. A working out of the figures in this connection will establish that the postmasters are bearing from thirty to forty per cent of the expenses of the reduction so appreciated by the public. This appears to be an altogether undue proportion.
The introduction of the postal note system has increased the amount of labour out of proportion to the revenue attached. This method of remitting small amounts (chiefly to the city offices) has largely curtailed the sale of stamps, which were formerly used. At offices where customs parcels are handled and distributed by mail to smaller offices, stamps are usually sent in payment of duty, and cash is remitted to port of entry, again curtailing

the sale of stamps received from the department.	...
2.	An examination! into that method of handling customs parcels and the remuneration (even where any is allowed) will reveal the fact that the work actually required to be performed, which is considerable, is practically unpaid for. This is one of the points which we desire to bring to your attention, that unremunerative work of this sort is being multiplied, while the revenue of the office is being held down by reduced rates of postage.
3.	In a number of the offices, besides keeping the office open throughout the regulation hours, the postmasters are compelled to await the arrival of a late evening train, and again in some instances have to get up at five or six o'clock in the morning to despatch a mail, thus imposing unduly long hours of service, without any allowances for any class of assistance, to say nothing of a competent assistant. In some offices, owing to the arrival of several different mails, the public is entitled to call and demand individual attention several times during the day, whereas the basis of remuneration makes no special provision for this. In places where tri-weekly trains carry the mails, the postmaster is compelled to remain (if he would give the public anything approaching satisfactory service), to provide, for a portion of three days a week, one or more duly qualified assistants. His allowance is inadequate for his own support at present cost of living, thus providing nothing for the payment of assistants.
4.	In view of the amount of mail matter to be re-sorted and forwarded, the forwarding allowances do not begin to pay for ^ the work done or the extra office room required. Another department with a deficit.
5.	The allowance for rent, fuel and light is decidedly inadequate. In practically every town where the post office is kept in a separate compartment, the room occupied could be leased for a rental in excess of the full allowance for rent, for heating and for lighting. In the town of Morris, the postmaster is allowed $100 for rent, fuel and light. For less space in the same building he receives from the Merchants Bank $350- a year for rent alone. At Melita the postmaster cancelled a lease bringing him a net annual rental of $180 to use the building for post office purposes on an allowance of $125 for rent, fuel and light. Other similar examples could be cited. Fuel and light are costly here.
fi. In the matter of securing proper assistants, we would point out that labour readily commands far larger remuneration in any market than it did a few years ago. To have experienced help available is a severe drain upon the limited exchequer of the postmaster who is unfortunate enough to require it, as nearly all do. Even where help is not regularly required, competent assistance must be had, if the postmaster is ever to seek recreation or relief from duty.
7. There is another matter which affects postmasters in the west more particularly, namely, the increased cost of living. This has frequently been brought to the attention of yourself and colleagues in various ways, and we note that already you have conceded the point, as in the case of the 20 per cent increase allowed the letter-carriers of Winnipeg. In our opinion, this does not represent the actual amount of difference, but is a recognition of that difference. In all lines the cost of living has advanced during
the past few years, while the postmasters are receiving less pay for more work.
8. A comparison with salaries paid in other departments of the public service, and even in other departments of the postal service, give an idea of our disadvantages. For example: First-class railway mail clerks receive $960 and mileage; second-class clerks, $880 and mileage. In the city of Winnipeg, the assistant postmaster gets $2,000 ; first-class clerks, $1,500 ; second class, $1,320 ; third class, $880, and letter-carries, $720. We do not think these are too highly paid, but an office with a revenue of $2,000 not only absorbs all of one person's time, but requires an additional c)erk at least a portion of the year. The postmaster of such an office receives for salary, commissions and allowances an average of less than $700, or less than half the amount received by a first-class city clerk, $100 less than a second-class railway mail clerk, and a trifle less than is paid to the city letter-carriers, and out of this modest income he must employ whatever additional help is required, and furnish a suitable office and office equipment. In most cases, his hours are longer and his responsibilities greater than those of any of the officials referred to. In one town, where the train arrived late and departed early, the postmaster until recently received $3.50 per month for overtime, while the railway agent received $19 a month extra.
In view of the conditions and facts set forth above, we would respectfully suggest the following changes, as tending to bring about a redress of our grievances :-1st. That the straight salary allowance be based on 50 per cent on the first $1,000 worth of stamps sold, and 40 per cent on all additional sales. This would barely offset the loss resulting from the reduction of letter postage. 2nd. That in Manitoba a special increase of at least 20 per cent be allowed to cover extra cost of living. 3rd. That the allowance for rent, fuel and light be doubled, so as to provide a reasonable rent for the office, and a provision for the cost of fuel and light in this country. 4th. That the money-order system be simplified, so as to lessen the amount of work to be performed for the small remuneration allowed, and also to increase its popularity with the business public, who now object to the restrictions hedging it round. 5th. In addition to the regular and general scale of allowances, we would request that a special allowance bo granted for each extra mail which tends to bring the public again before the wicket for individual attention during the day ; that the forward allowance be materially increased to distributing offices ; that a special allowance be given to postmasters who are compelled to work before 8 a.m., or after 7 p.m. Among the mechanical industries the special allowance for overtime is very marked. That in the case of offices where mails are so infrequent as to have large quantities of mail matter delivered at the office at one time, so that the public convenience really requires the employment of one or more assistants, an allowance be given towards the payment of such assistant or assistants.
6th. In addition to the above, we feel that there are a number of cases of special minor grievances which we cannot enter into in detail, but in which we tljink that a little investigation would show that redress could be effected, so as to relieve the postmasters concerned, without in any way impairing the efficiency and safety of the public service, which grievances have probably continued to exist

because they have not been brought to your honourable attention.
And we would respectfully urge that the above matters be duly considered, and that a large measure of redress be granted in the very near future.
And your petitioners, as in duty bound, will ever pray.

maintopic: MANITOBA AND NORTH-WEST ACCOUNTING POSTMASTERS' ASSOCIATION.

speechtext:
Supplementary suggestions passed by Executive.
1.	That all accounting offices be given an allowance for rent, fuel and light.
2.	That twine, mucilage, pens, ink', pencils, &c., for post office use be furnished by the department, and not at the expense of the postmaster, as at present.
3.	That the department make it more clear to all publishers that newspapers must be suitably folded and that they must be addressed plainly. That where labels are used, they must be in large, clear type, and that if possible, uniformity of colour in labels be secured.
4.	That a full list of ' Suggestions to the Public ' be printed by the department and supplied to all postmasters for display in their offices, as tending to make it clear that certain regulations are found necessary by the department, and are not based on the caprice or convenience of the postmaster. For instance, that stamps and money-orders may be purchased during the distribution of a newly arrived mail, and that money-orders and postal notes are not available for purchase after the registered mail closes for an outgoing mail. Also, some suggestions as to the age of children who are to be considered as proper persons to receive mail from the wicket.
5.	That when instructions are sent out for the weighing of all mails, that facilities for such weighing be afforded by the department.
6.	That in view of the large sums of money at times in the mails in this country, and hence often stored in the post office, and in view of the value of the stamps and the importance of the books now to be kept, that safes ' be provided for accounting postmasters, or an allowance be granted to pay for use of same, when provided by the postmaster.
2. Is it the intention to accede to the request of the association ?

QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, before the Orders of the Day are called, I beg leave to rise to a question of privilege. On Wednesday last, Mr. Speaker, I drew your attention to the fact that 1 had serious doubts about the authenticity of the signatures of certain petitions which were presented in this House in opposition to the construction of a new transcontinental railway. You were kind enough to tell me and tell this House that the hon. members who presented these petitions assumed in so doing full responsibility for everything in connection with these petitions. 1 had them published in the newspapers of the district in order to make sure whether my doubts were founded or not. I am now in a position to prove to this House and to the country that a very grave abuse of the honour and dignity of this parliament has been committed, and

Mr. TALBOT-the wholesale forgery

speechtext:
These are notes of my own written by my own hand-and the wholesale
forgery has been committed by over zealous partisans urged by unscrupulous though important newspapers of Montreal. These petitions contain the names of mere boys, names of people who live in the United States, names of people who have been dead for years, names of people who are in lunatic asylums, names of people, who, owinig to their advanced age, are absolutely irresponsible, names of people who knew nothing of these petitions and names of people who when asked to sign positively refused. In view of these facts which I am in a position to prove, I beg, Mr. Speaker, to submit a motion to the consideration of the House. My reason for doing so is that I consider that the right of petition is sacred, and I do not question for a moment the right of the gentlemen who signed the petitions to present and emphasize their objections to the government policy on this transcontinental railway question in that way if they chose to do so, but for my part, and I feel sure that this honourable House will endorse me, I must enter my most solemn protest against this audacious and monstrous attempt to impose upon the good faith of parliament and the country, by seeking to create the utterly false and erroneous impression that the people in the province of Quebec at least are opposed to this great national undertaking, and I say that it is a screaming farce and a most shameful departure from all principles of honour and dignity due to this parliament to present such petitions.

false pretenses, to create a wrong impression. My hon. friend from Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) may pei'haps have spoken warmly. speechtext: I consider this a much more serious matter than it at first appeared to be. Following him, the right hon. the First Minister insinuates that all the petitions against the railway were of a similar character. Under these circumstances, it becomes a matter of the gravest importance that the inquiry should be of the very widest and most general character. From what I know of the signers of some of these petitions, I believe them to be men of high integrity and of sterling character, and so far as I know the petitions are truthfully and honestly signed. But the stigma cast upon these petitions by the right hon. First Minister applies to every petition which has been presented to this House, and therefore it involves the necessity of bringing the individual signers before the committee ; and I demand, in the interest of justice and fair-play, and for the vindication of the character of the Reformers as well as the Conservatives who signed these petitions, that they be brought before that committee to give their testimony. It is too important to allow it to pass in that way, after the specific allegations of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) that the signatures to these petitions were forgeries or signed by lunatics or aged people or people 'who were dead, especially we have the statement of the right hon. the First Minister, immediately following, that the petitions generally were of the same character. I have had the honour of presenting a few petitions from the province of Ontario and I have some others which I have not yet presented. The right hon. the Prime Minister has insinuated that a very large number of the petitions have been falsely signed. I wish to say that I would like to have an investigation into the petitions which I presented from the electors of my county, and I would insist that the scope of this investigation be sufficiently wide to allow every man who signed
one of these petitions to come here and make a declaration. I did not go closely into every petition which I presented, nor was it my duty to do so, but I have sufficient confidence in the electors of my county to feel assured that no signature is other than genuine. That is the way we do business in Ontario. Hon. gentlemen opposite laugh. They do not seem to care how long the session may last and I suppose we need not worry very much about it. I wish to say that I am in favour of the motion moved by the other side in so far as it goes. I am in favour of a complete investigation into this whole matter, but I am still more in favour of the resolution introduced by the hon. member for West Toronto (Mr. Clarke), that every petition presented to this House shall go before this committee and there shall be a complete investigation, so that the people will understand whether or not any of these signatures are false. I regard this as a most important question. Even at this late stage of the session, whether it should take several months or not, it is in the interest of the public that we should have an honest and complete investigation into the signatures to the petitions against this government project of a transcontinental railway.

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: I had the honour, Mr. Speaker, of presenting several petitions. The first petition which I presented was accompanied with a letter stating that I would find on examination that it had been signed by Reformers and Conservatives alike. On glancing over the names, I found that statement correct, and I believe the same remark would apply to all the petitions I presented to this House.

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext:
As it is concerning some petitions which I presented that controversy has arisen, I wish to state, Mr. Speaker, that I presented these petitions in the utmost good faith and belief that they were perfectly regular. And, Mr. Speaker, apart from the utterly unsupported statement of the hon. njember for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) we have no evidence whatever that there is anything irregular about them. In presenting these petitions I submit that I was certainly more warranted in assuming that the signatures were bona fide and genuine than the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) was in making use of the outrageously extreme language he has. After a reference which had been made by that hon. gentleman to these petitions in this House on a former occasion, I had a conversation with him, in which t called his attention to the fact that if some of the signatures were apparently written by the same hand, that gave no one any right to assume that they were not written in good faith at the request of the people who were not able to write their own names. In the rural parts of our provinces, it is not unusual to find electors who can-

not sign their names, and we are entitled to assume that the signatures of such electors to these petitions were written by people who were authorized to sign for them. Hon. gentlemen know that the most solemn document a man signs in the course of his life (his will) is not necessarily signed by his own hand. He has a perfect right to ask his friend or neighbour to sign it for him. The excuse made by the hon. member for Belle-cliasse was that in each such case there should have been a witness who should have made a statutory declaration affirming that he was present and saw the signature made by 1he person who was requested to make it. Well, Sir, I am not aware that there is any procedure laid down in the rules of this House requiring any such thing to be done, and the House will well understand that it would not be practicable. It seems to me that, in the absence of any evidence to the contrary, this House is bound to assume that the signatures were genuine. Until some direct evidence is produced showing some fraud in the affixing of signatures, no one has the right to challenge their authenticity. Until evidence is produced before the committee of investigation, under oath, establishing fraud, we are bound to assume that everything is absolutely regular. I do not propose to make any statement with regard to these petitions now if they are to go before a committee and be investigated ; but so far as I am concerned, I take this opportunity of cordially inviting any investigation into any connection I have had with these matters. Every hon. gentleman on this side is most anxious that all the facts and proceedings should be investigated in the fullest manner. If the hon. member for Bellechasse means to insinuate that I had reason to suspect or believe that there was anything appearing on the face of either of the petitions I presented which should have led me to investigate into their genuineness, then I throw that insinuation back to the hon. gentleman with the scorn it deserves. So far as I am concerned, X repeat, T invite tl,ie fullest investigation.

In one polling division, in which there were only 115 names on the voters' list, no less than 114 votes were

recorded. No man is so idiotic as to believe that, in such a polling division, 114 electors actually presented themselves and voted. In another division of the city of Quebec, I find that 111 votes were polled out of 114 names on the list. And, with a zeal worthy of their masters in the province of Quebec, where they were trying to get a negative vote on the plebiscite, in Quebec Centre, they did the magnificent work against the cause of temperance of polling 105 votes where there were only 101 names on the list. And you can take the province of Quebec county by county, and find evidences of such frauds as are exposed by the figures I have just read.

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: I am much surprised at the right lion. Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier) backing up so strongly the resolution of the hon. member for Bellecbasse (Mr. Talbot). When these petitions were being presented to the House day by day, signed by men of both parties throughout the Dominion, the Liberal papers all over the country tried to create the impression that the petitions were only from members of the Conservative party. They tried to make the petitions fall flat. Now, when this Grand Trunk Pacific Bill was being put through this House, we on this side felt it our duty to do everything we possibly could to prevent it becoming law without an opportunity being afforded of discussing it before the people, so that they might be educated on the question and understand what was before them. If the right hon. Prime Minister will actually carry through this investigation that has been proposed- I for one do not believe that he has any intention whatever of doing so-he will find that this Grand Trunk Pacific Bill is being opposed by leading Liberals from one end of the country to the other. If that investigation is properly held, I am satisfied that leading Liberals from every constituency of this Dominion will declare themselves opposed to the Prime Minister's policy, and in this way he will gain some idea of the effect that this Grand Trunk Pacific Bill will have upon his party at the next general election. I feel, for one, that this is the opportunity of our life to show to the people the folly of having the Grand Trunk Bill pressed through the House during the present session. I hope, therefore, that the right hon. Prime Minister has not had this motion proposed as a sham, but that he will give us the very fullest investigation, even if we take another six months to carry it out.

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: It is quite clear that the government are at sea, perfectly at sea, as regards public opinion in the province of Ontario on the subject of this proposed transcontinental railway. I may say that one of the petitions sent to me was accompanied with a letter from the sender stating that every man he asked to sign it had signed1 it cheerfully, and there were as many Liberals as Conservatives on the petition. I am satisfied that every name on the petition is right. And I ask yon, Mr. Speaker, why should not any man, no matter what his politics, be glad to sign such a petition? The most important request in that petition is that the construction of this road should not be proceeded with until proper surveys had been prepared. Why, the exMinister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair), whom I am glad to see in his place, stated that one of the chief reasons why he broke with his colleagues on this question was this very reason. And if that hon. gentleman thought this of sufficient importance to be one of his chief reasons for leaving the government, why should any Liberal in Ontario or any other province, object to signing these petitions. I think the government have not realized their position in this matter, but an appeal to the people which I hope they will soon grant, will convince them of the opinion of the country.

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext:
As one of those who had the honour of presenting some of the petitions referred to, I desire, in the strongest possible manner, to resent the imputation cast upon the signatures of these petitions as not being genuine, by no less a personage than the right hon. Prime Minister of this country. The hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. McCreary) presented a petition signed by 800 residents of the province of Manitoba against the railway rates on cream and other products. The hon. gentleman (Mr. McCreary) assumes responsibility for the genuineness of that petition. He has faith, as I have, that the signatures are genuine. We who are representatives are only doing our duty in presenting these petitions to parliament, and we cannot be responsible for every single individual name that is on them. We cannot answer for the genuineness of all these names, but at any rate, we in the province of Manitoba feel such confidence in the integrity and in the honesty of our inhabitants that we know well that they would resort to no such despicable methods as those which the member for Bellechasse states were resorted to in connection with the signing of those petitions in the province of Quebec. Now, I do not know so much about the inhabitants of that gentleman's province as he knows himself, but certainly, coming as I do from the west, I believe it to be beneath my dignity to cast such aspersions upon the inhabitants of Quebec as have emanated from that hon. gentleman himself. The most amusing thing, Mr. Speaker, in connection with this whole affair, is to see the dignity of parliament being looked after by the hon. member for Bellechasse, who now constitutes himself a champion of the dignity of parliament I would say, to use a vulgarism,

tliat it was enough to make a horse laugh, if it were not so serious a matter. I think that no other gentleman on that side of the House could be found who would use such violent language and make such a serious charge against the gentlemen who have attached their signatures to these petitions. But I am not so much surprised at that hon. gentleman as I was at the Prime Minister, when he actually stated that no doubt these two petitions were samples of what prevailed throughout the whole Dominion. I say that it is my duty to rise and resent on thh part of the people of Manitoba, such an aspersion upon those who have attached their signatures to these petitions, and who, in sending them in, distinctly stated that they would have been much more numerously signed had they had time to circulate them a while longer. Now, Sir, like hon. gentlemen on that side of the House, we are in favour of an investigation, and we Insist on a full investigation, and are quite willing to stay here the balance of the year to get that investigation. The right hon. gentleman need not think that he can confine his investiation to two or three of these petitions, and then go through the country and raise a doubt of their genuineness, and proclaim that they are a sample of what took place in almost every province of the Dominion. It is, I say, an aspersion cast upon the inhabitants of our country who, though Conservatives in their politics, were they to-morrow to go over and give their support to the government on this transcontinental road or on their general policy, the Prime Minister would say that ' nothing would be too good for them,' as he said in regard to some of his colleagues in the past ; but when his colleagues left the administration and refused to support him on this railway question, now nothing is too bad for them. I say the mere fact of a man being a Conservative does not change his character to that extent that he becomes a forger immediately, and then as soon as he joins the Liberal party he becomes one of the best citizens of the country. I think we will find that this is a mere device on the part of the hon. member for Bellechasse, who no doubt, acting under instructions from the government, wanted to break the force of public opinion that has expressed itself against this Trans-Canada road and its prosecution under its present auspices. But I think the Prime Minister will find that he has mistaken public opinion when he attempts to gag and to stifle the opinion of this country by asserting that these signatures were not genuine, when as a matter of fact they would have been far more numerous had time and opportunity been given.

If the remark's had ended with the hon. member for Bellechasse X do not think I would have been called upon to say anything, but when the right bon. leader of the government (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) [DOT]practically insinuated that the statements made by the hon. member for Bellechasse in regard to these two petitions were also true in regard to all the petitions filed, I feel that it is my duty to say something in regard to that statement. Now, is it to be said that the people are insane because they have signed a petition, the second clause of which states that :
Your petitioners are of the opinion that it would be unwise and imprudent to take definite action until the government and parliament are fully possessed of the information essential to a proper decision of the question?
The hon. member. for Bellechasse says that insane people have signed that petition in which that statement is embodied. He might as well have said that the hon. exMinister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) was insane when he made this statement :
But I am not in favour of impetuously rushing into the construction of a transcontinental line from Quebec, through an unknown country to .Winnipeg and west until we know something about it-until we have the fullest information about it. The project is one of very great magnitude and it should be dealt with only after the maturest deliberation.
The 'lion. ex-Minfeter of Railways and Canals has put it in very much stronger terms than the language of this petition. I think the amendment moved by my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Clarke) is a proper amendment, and now that the right hon. Prime Minister has intimated or insinuated that all these petitions have false signatures, that they have been signed by dead men and have been signed by insane people, we have the right to have all these petitions thoroughly investigated, no matter how long it may take us.

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had the honour of presenting some of these petitions, and when the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) attacked two of them, I thought it was very proper to do so if he had reasonable grounds. But of the hundreds of petitions that have been presented there is not the slightest charge that there is any informality or incorrectness in them, with the exception of these two. For the right hon. Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) to arise when only two petitions were attacked, and these two in reference to some three or four names, and make the wholesale charge which he heralded against the hundreds of men who had signed all of the other petitions without a scintilla of evidence, is one of the most extraordinary things that I ever heard of. I think the right hon. gen-

tlemau should, he a man of more discretion and judgment than to be carried away by a momentary impulse to make a statement of such a startling character. The right of petition is one of the most sacred rights that we have. Everybody has the right to come to this parliament and present a petition. It is one of the most cherished rights that we have, and a right to secure which wars have been waged in England. I agree that a member of parliament must be responsible for his petitions, but I say that he must be responsible in a reasonable and intelligent manner. If a petition is sent from my county professing to be signed by the electors of the county, I would present it in the utmost good faith, believing that everything was correct and honourable. The hon. member for Bellechasse has made the most extraordinary charge against this government that has ever been made since I have been in parliament. According to his own story, so unpopular and hated has this government become in the province of Quebec that men leave their graves and walk abroad to sign petitions against it. Even the asylums have been invaded by the awful terror of the existence of this government, because the crazy men in the province of Quebec have been frightened by the intolerable methods of this government into moments of sanity and lucidity, when they apparently petition this House to save them from the recklessness of this government. It strikes me that the hon. member for Bellechasse has levelled the most deadly blow against this government that has been levelled against it, when he says that men who have left the cares of life and sought quiet in the grave rise up to enter their protest against the infamy of this government. Why, Sir, the right hon. Prime Minister, if he had been an astute man, would have at once repudiated the language of the hon. member for Bellechasse, and asked him to desist, because he was pointing to a state of affairs which showed that petitions ought to be levelled by every live man against this measure when the dead have risen from their graves to protest against it. Now, gentlemen-

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: Now, Mr. Speaker-hon. gentlemen opposite are so extremely polite and courteous that an hon. gentleman cannot be permitted the slightest deviation from the rule, even if he does happen to be a young member-this method of attacking petitions should have the reprobation of this House. The charge should have been levelled against one, or two, or three names; the charge should have been specific ; because, when you attack the general right of petition, you strike at one of the most sacred rights and privileges of the country, and while I agree that no man should offer to insult this parliament by pretending to

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: petition it when he does not really sign his name or agree to somebody else signing it, while I concur that it was a most serious matter for any man to present a petition containing a single name that he does not know to be genuine, I think when petitions are presented here they should be assumed to be regularly and honestly signed, because it would be a serious attack upon the reputation and decency of the people and upon their intelligence to fancy that anybody in the country could be wild and bad enough to obtain the signatures of men improperly ; and, secondly, when obtained that they should be presented to this parliament. Therefore, when the hon. member for Bellechasse attacks these petitions he charges, first, that there was some man in this country bad enough to go round and ask men to sign their names to petitions, and when they would not .do so to sit down deliberately and commit forgery. That is a charge against the honour and honesty of the people of this country that does not apply, I am glad to say, against the province of Nova Scotia. If it can be applied to any other province, I can tell the House that there is not a man in the province of Nova Scotia bad enough to do that kind of thing, and when an hon. member makes such a charge in regard to the province of Quebec, I say that he insults the province of Quebec. I repudiate it on behalf of the province of Quebec. I do not believe there is any man who would be bad enough in the province of Quebec to go around and forge the signature of his neighbours to a petition and to send it to this parliament to have it presented. For my part, on behalf of the province of Quebec, I refuse to believe that a single name to these petitions was signed improperly. Therefore, when the hon. member, knowing the sacredness of the right of petition, made his Charges, he should have particularized what names he believed to be bad, so that the whole character of all the petitioners should not have been assailed. It is an extraordinary and an incredible position for the government to take. The Prime Minister should have been the first to denounce this attack upon the honour of thousands and thousands of the electorate of this country. It is impossible to believe that thousands of our citizens are tainted with forgery, fraud and criminality. I refuse to believe if, and the Prime Minister should have been the first to refuse to believe it. The member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) has a perfect right to make the charge, but he ought to make it with the utmost gravity, the utmost care, the utmost particularity, and he should not have cast a slur on the whole body of the citizens of Canada who signed these petitions.

And what is seventeen out of thousands ? There are three or four

hundred criminals in our penitentiaries, but does that asperse the high moral character of all the citizens of Canada ?

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: Seventeen out of twenty-four.

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: And supposing it is true that seventeen are bad, I will decline to believe that because that is the case all the citizens of Quebec, who signed these petitions, are guilty of fraud and forgery. The hon. member (Mr. Talbot) should have been most guarded to confine his charges simply to the names which he thinks are bad, and the Prime Minister should have himself guarded the reputation of the people of Canada by demanding that these charges should be particularized. Even if some names should be found to be bad, then we must assume that the person who had charge of the signatures for that petition was not careful in having it signed. That is all it would amount to. I support the amendment of the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Clarke) that all of these petitions be brought before this committee, in order that the fair name of the people of Canada may be safe from the serious charge made against them, and which charge has been endorsed by the Prime Minister.

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: I had the honour of presenting some of these petitions, and I desire to say that so far as I know, I believe the signatures to them are genuine in every respect. I do not wonder at an attempt being made by the Liberals in this House to discredit those who petitioned against the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway, in view of the manner in which they have attempted to discredit a late minister of the government whom they supported, who had the courage to protest against the ridiculous idea of building this railway without plans, and without necessary information. These gentlemen opposite have endeavoured in every way to belittle the ex-Minis'ter of Railways (Hon. Mr. Blair), and I have not the slightest doubt they would belittle him more if they were able to. The hon. member for Bellecbasse (Mr. Talbot) is put up to this scheme to try to blackmail the petitioners all through this Dominion of Canada. It is no wonder, I repeat, that they try to blacken the character of the petitioners, just as they tried to blacken the ex-Minister of Railways, who they said was not fit to unloose the shoe-laces of the Prime Minister. Although I did not see the signatures upon the petitions which I had the honour to present, I believe that every name on them was legitimately put there with the knowledge of the persons who signed. I want all the men who signed this petition in tire county of Dufferin, to be summoned down here, so as to give them an opportunity of stating before parliament, whether they signed these petitions or not. If there is any fair-play in the matter, the government will afford these petitioners this opportunity.

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: We have not been treated this morning to a very edifying spectacle in connection with the charge which has been made by our friend from Bellecbasse (Mr. Talbot). speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I will withdraw any expression which our hon. friends on the other side think is offensive ; but I will go on to say that when the sacred right of petition is prostituted for political purposes-that is what I said, and that is what I say still. If certain disaffected people anywhere in this country have a grievance, they have a perfect right to petition this House to have that grievance removed. But when in a newspaper office, or in a gathering of politicians somewhere or somehow in the darkness of tlnj night, a scheme is set on foot for petitions headed in a certain way to be sent throughout the length and breadith of this country, to create the idea that these petitioners have a grievance; and when these petitions are being hawked about from pillar to post; and when, as is represented here, they are fraudulently signed; when the dead, as our hon. friend says, are brought from their graves and others are brought from lunatic asylums, when all other conceivable methods are used to get these petitions signed-what is it for ? Not because these people have a grievance, but to give our hon. friends opposite a political card to play in the coming elections; because they want to trump up the idea that there is a great protest against this railway throughout the country. I erxcuse our hon. friends on the other side from knowingly presenting these fraudulent petitions. They could not possibly know who signed them or how they were obtained. I have not the slightest doubt that if one had reached me from my own constituency, I would have presented it in good faith. But do not let our hon. friends opposite run away with the impression that they are going to convince the public that there was no fraud in any particular instance.

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext:
There is no doubt that our hon. friend from Brant (Mr. Heyd) maintains a very lofty view as to the character of the citizens of this country and the members of this House. He seems to have no higher opinion of them than to assume that the citizens of this country are on the lookout for a cheap ride to Ottawa. I congratulate the hon. gentleman on showing that be possesses those qualities of statesmanship which justify his presence in this House. I hope it will not be presumed that the members of this House generally are represented by the hon. gentleman. I would like to think that he represents himself alone in speaking in the way he has done. With that remark. I think I might let the Mr. BELL.
opinion of the hon. gentleman go to the oblivion to which it properly belongs. I may say that several petitions in connection with this matter were presented to this House by myself in perfect good, faith. I do not know that all the signatures attached to them were put there by the parties who purport to have signed them, and I do not know that the Prime Minister would ask any member of this House to give any such assurance in presenting a petition. But I do think that the right hon. gentleman, in making the charge which lie has made in his place in this House, against the people of Canada generally, and against the citizens of his own province, spoke much too hastily and without much reflection as to the importance of the words he uttered. There was in the right hon. gentleman's remarks the implication that possibly a large proportion of the signatures on the petitions presented to this House were forgeries ; which implied such a charge against the people of this country as no Prime Minister of Canada should ever dare to make in the House of Commons. The right of petition belongs to us ns British subjects ; and how are our petitions to be presented except through the representatives of the people who have seats in this House ? If it can be shown that in some cases that privilege has been abused, I am sure the right hon. gentleman will find that no men in this House are more anxious to discover the wrong and have it rectified than the gentlemen sitting on this side of the House. But we decline to allow the right hon. gentleman to put up one of his followers on the back benches, with a prepared case, to cast discredit on hundreds and thousands of these petitioners, and to decline to allow a more general investigation to be made. If the right hon. gentleman feels that he can accuse the people of Canada generally of this kind of wrong-doing, we will declare on our part that the people of Canada must have the right of rebutting that charge, and throwing it back in the right hon. gentleman's face. The intention of hon. gentlemen on the government side of the House, is to cast doubt on the whole series of petitions.

Blair, ex-Minister of Railways and Canals, irecent-ly a colleague of the right lion, gentleman, who not only, to all intents and purposes, signed his name to the petition, but enforced it in a powerful arraignment of the government, which I may say has not to this moment been replied to by any member of the government. site attempt to belittle the protest of the people of Canada against this outrage ; but that attempt will fail, and fail most effectually. It is a very small trick on the part of the government to put up a gentleman who in the early part of the sess-sion

I do not desire to cast any suspicion. I merely suggested what I thought was a very obvious fact-that something must have transpired. If my remark in that very mild form is objectionable, I am willing to withdraw it. But you find the government compelled to resort to these efforts to try to weaken the attack made upon them in the only way in which it can be made by means of petitions. I have a petition from the county of Cumberland, which I am assured by the gentleman who sent it to me, would have been signed by 80 per cent of the electors, if he could only have had sufficient time to present it for signature. There are petitions which as we will be only too happy to prove, have been signed by men who, in other respects, are supporting the present government, but who, so far as this most grotesque railway project is concerned, are opposed to the government. If the right hon. geutleman wants to weaken the force of these petitions, he is not going to do it by attacking one here and there, but he must treat the whole together. What was the course taken by hon. gentlemen opposite last session when they sought to throw discredit on the census
returns of the province of Quebec ? The right hon. gentleman laid on the Table a great mass of evidence intended to show that there was an improper computation of the population of the province of Quebec in the census of 1891- He was challenged by this side not to rely solely ou such evidence as he could procure from his partisans throughout that province, but to submit the whole matter to the investigation of some competent authority. Did he do it ? No, Sir, he did as he did in the case of the West Huron election frauds. He refused to have the matter investigated by a competent tribunal. Just as he does in every difficult situation in which he finds himself, he managed to make use of some subterfuge and creep out when challenged. But if now, after he is challenged to have a full inquiry, he prefers to shirk his duty, he can only do so in defiance of the protest of the opposition.

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext: ' There can be no doubt, Mr. Speaker, about the fact that the opposition have lost their self-control.

maintopic: QUESTION OF PRIVILEGE-PETITIONS AGAINST NATIONAL TRANSCONTINENTAL RAILWAY.
speechtext:
They have made their last throw and lost. A few weeks ago, with the aid of a Canadian newspaper they determined to put forth a propaganda which they thought would sweep the whole country. They were going to submerge this House with a deluge of petitions and completely overpower the government. But what has been the result ? After trying their utmost, after canvassing constituencies, after begging the people to sign, they have induced less than four per cent of the electorate to sign petitions against the government railway project; and among that four per cent are lunatics and dead men and men who are not living in the country at all. They have ignominiously failed to get the petitions signed, which they have been hawking around for weeks. My hon. friend from Pictou (Mr. Bell) says that he could have had eighty per cent of the people in some districts of Cumberland to sign the petition which he presented. Let me tell the hon. gentleman that there are 40,000 people in that constituency, and that his friends who went through it from house to house got just 151 names out of these 40,000. Does that look like 80 per cent of the people? I was down in my constituency a few weeks ago, and during my stay I did not find one Liberal who did not approve of the government scheme, and I met many Conservatives who said they were ashamed of their party, once led by such men as Sir John Macdonald and Sir Charles Tupper-a party which then had the instincts of government, but which now has sunk so low as to oppose our national development. I can tell my hon friend further that he might tramp the county of Cumberland from end to end, and he would not get one per cent of the people in the

Liberal ranks to sign any petition in favour of the alternative scheme of the leader of the opposition. These lion, gentlemen opposite have tried to use the ex-Minister of Railways to bolster up their case, but we know that that bon. gentleman has freely expressed his opinion that the alternative proposition of the leader of the opposition is absolutely ridiculous and would not be entertained by* the people. Have any petitions been presented in favour of that alternative scheme ? Not a single one. My hon. friend from Belleehasse (Mr. Talbot) has presented specific charges regarding certain petitions and has been answered by a volume of abuse, and no doubt I shall be treated in like manner. These hon. gentlemen resort to the old dodge of abusing the opposing attorney in default of argument. In one of the petitions there are thirty out of thirty-four names written in the one handwriting. Let me tell the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) that although I do not believe that there was forgery in my con-' stituency, these 151 names were not signed by 151 different hands. There are several in the same handwriting. What are the facts ? These gentlemen opposite prepared these petitions in conjunction with a certain newspaper and sent them broadcast over the country. Did these petitions ask the people of Canada to declare that this road should not be built ? No, Sir. I have in my hand a copy of two of them, one prepared to circulate in the east and one for circulation in the west, and the one differs from the other as black from white. Here is the petition from the east, which was presented for signature in the county of Cumberland. It sets forth :
That your petitioners are of opinion that it would be unwise and imprudent to take definite action until the government and parliament are fully possessed of the information essential to a proper decision of that question.
That a project of such magnitude should not be undertaken without the most complete and accurate surveys, under the direction and control of engineers of standing and repute.
But you will uot find any such paragraph with western petitions.
That such surveys should be in the hands of the government and of parliament before the credit of the Dominion is committed to an enterprise which involves enormous obligations.
That, however, the most competent men are of opinion that the cost of the projected line between Winnipeg and Moncton will reach the enormous amount of upwards of $120,000,000.
That, on the contrary, it is to he greatly feared that by pledging the credit of the country to such a vast extent, the government will make it impossible to carry out works better calculated to meet the transportation needs of the country.
This is equivalent to saying that if the government go ahead with this project, there will be no public money available to build other railways. Then it proceeds to say : Mr. LOGAN.
That the government, parliament and the taxpayers should hanve an opportunity to learn the results of the investigation of the said commission ; and to examine the evidence upon which such results were arrived at.
That is the eastern petition. Let us now look at the western petition. It starts out by stating that transportation facilities are necessary and then proceeds to say :
. That the over capitalization of transporta-tiou companies is one of the most important conditions leading to unduly high rates, and should be prevented.
That a railway system designed to move the products of the west should not be burdened by the addition of costly and needless sections ; that the proposed eastern section of the Grand Trunk Pacific would be of value chiefly for the purpose of colonizing the territory it traverses ; and that western lines should not be obliged to impose rates fixed with a view of providing for the annual fixed charges upon such section, between one and two thousand miles long, built many years in advance of settlement in the James bay basin.
That the company should not be committed to the construction of the eastern section.
This is the petition presented to the west.

That the proposed western section of the Grand Trunk Pacific, from Winnipeg to Edmonton should be constructed as an additional line opening up new- territory ; and that the Grand Trunk Pacific Company should not be allow-ed to purchase the Canadian Northern

Mr. Speaker, the petition which was presented in the House from the eastern part of Canada, and which they failed to get signed by any material part of the population of that part of Canada was put upon this ground-the people were asked to sign it on the ground that 8120,000,000 would have to be paid for the construction of this road, that this would be taken out of the treasury, and that the effect of its expenditure would be to prevent facilities being provided which were required in that part of the country, in the petitions presented in the western part of Canada this was not mentioned, but signatures were sought to the petition on the ground that the road would be too heavily bonded and would be compelled to charge too high rates. I charge that these petitions were prepared in Eastern Canada, either in the city of Montreal or in the city of Ottawa; that one form of petition was sent to the eastern part of Canada [DOT] to be signed and the other sent to the western part of Canada to be signed; and not four per cent of the electorate of Canada signed either one petition or the other.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I am one of the members of the House who presented petitions in regard to this much vexed and much discussed railway project of the government, I desire that this discussion shall not close without a word from me on the subject. I should not have troubled the House at all if the matter had ended with the remarks of the hon. member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot). But, when the Prime Minister, undertaking to represent the whole country and standing for the advisers of His Ex-1 eellency the Governor General in all administrative matters carried the argument to the distance he did this morning in the few remarks with which he favoured the House, I feel that it is incumbent upon me not only on my own part, but out of respect and consideration for the electors whom I represent who have hitherto supported this government and voted against me in the last election, to say a few words. I say it is my duty, not speaking alone for members of the opposition, or even for those in my county who are in the habit of voting for
the Liberal Conservative party, but speaking for those who have hitherto voted for the so-called Reform party and the government now in power, to say a word in refutation and repudiation of the insinuation thrown out by the right hon. Prime Minister. The hon. member for Bellechasse undertook, from information which he seemed to think satisfactory-and perhaps he is to be excused, fox-, as the Prime Minister said, the hon. gentleman is not a lawyer and does not know the value of evidence-to find fault with one or two ixetitions in regard to this matter which has come from certain places in the province in which iie resides. The hon. member for Bellechasse attacks certain parts of that province in attacking the petitions which come from it. He undertook, as I say, on the strength of information which satisfies him that there is something wrong in these petitions io ask an investigation in regard to these two-I believe there were two-petitions to which he refers. It might well have stooped there, and I think it ought to have stopped there. The hon. member for Bellechasse might or might not have been entitled by the evidence which he presented to prolong the session of this House and have an investigation cai'ried on. While I notice that the hon. member for Bellechasse was very anxious to have an investigation, he based his demand for it largely upon the fact that several signatures in the petitions were in the same handwriting. As the hon. gentleman (Mr. Talbot) is not a lawyer, I might be permitted to point out that this of itself is not a piece of. fraud. His province, no doubt, is in the same position as others in this matter. There are men who cannot write, or men who do not put their own names to petitions, but l'equest another person to sign for them. There are persons who cannot write their names legibly and, if they wish to petition parliament or petition a municipal body or any other authority must have their names written by others. It may be that the hon. member for Bellechasse will find that this is the mare s nest he has discovered. But that is not the most serious part of it, nor would the remarks of the hon. member for Bellechasse with regard to petitions from his own province have caused me to feel it my duty to speak, But I rise, as I have said, to repudiate the insinuations thrown out by the right hon. Prime Minister against all the petitions that have been presented against this measure. The petitions from the county of Lincoln were presented by me in good faith. They were signed by persons whom I know. I read every signature and I can assure the Prime Minister and every member of parliament that several names, in the petitioner s own handwriting, are the names of gentlemen who have never voted against the party of the present government, but who will not be the more inclined to vote for that party by the insult of the Prime Minister,

is supposed to have got his signature is involved, the honour of the man who sent the petition to me and asked me to present it to this House is involved and I say that these men must come down here, whether they have a free ride or not, as the hon. member for South Brant (Mr. Heyd) states, and say where these petitions came from. Therefore, I say the investigation must be as wide as that which has been suggested by my hon. friend? from West Toronto, and it is the right hon. gentleman's fault if it does take time and involves expense.
I have just a word to say in regard to the hon. member for South Brant. He had the temerity to stand up and say that the idea of presenting these petitions was conceived in the darkness of night. I wondered when he said that if he thought that the project which the hon. ex-Minister of Railways and Canals (Hon. Mr. Blair) had condemned and which had caused him to leave the cabinet was conceived in day-light. Was there so much of the noon-day sun that the people of the country understood it ? Was it not because there was no light upon the subject that these petitions were presented here ? In spite of all that the opposition could do, representing the best interests of the people of Canada, to get information upon the subject that Bill was railroaded through this House as fast as they could put it through. Notwithstanding the fact that the opposition used every means in their power to get the information to try and And out -what obligation this was going to impose upon the country, they were unsuccessful, while at every step the evidence seemed to preponderate against the wisdom of the scheme. In spite of all that, in spite of the fact that Cox could not wait, in spite of the fact that the government were apparently bound to put it through, what did the people of Canada do ? In each county, wherever they could within the short time at their disposal, they prepared and sent petitions down here saying that:	If the government do not
think the members of the opposition were right in what they said, we ourselves petition as ordinary voters and ask you to delay until you get more information. The hon. member for South Brant should have reflected as to where and how this scheme originated. He ought to have asked himself whether he and other hon. gentlemen behind him had as much light upon the subject as they desired when the scheme was first announced ? Does he not know that several hon. gentlemen who voted for the government were at the beginning utterly opposed to it ? Does he not know that lots of the supporters of the present government in the country were waiting anxiously to have placed before them the merits of this question and that they have not yet received the light upon the subject that they ought to have received ? Does he not know that the men signing these petitions have declared that there is not the day-light upon Mr. LANCASTER.
the question that there ought to be before the country was involved in the enormous expenditure that this scheme will entail ?
The hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Logan) had a few words to say before one o'clock and he read a lecture to hon. members of the opposition as to what, from his standpoint, should be their duty in this House. He said that we on this side of the House, having no case, were abusing the members of the government. He said that having been disappointed in our last effort to impose our conclusions upon the government we were abusing the attorney representing the government on this question.
I do not think that we have been abusing the members of the government in this matter, but, I think that the government have abused the people who have signed these petitions. I do not think they have been fairly treated in the measure which has been meted out to them in regard to these petitions. He says that this is the opposition's last resort. It may be the opposition's last resort at the present time but it is not the opposition's last resort because the opposition's- last resort is the people's last resort. If the government have the courage to go before the country the hon. member for Cumberland will find that the opposition's last resort is to make the appeal that they shall make against the government, and he will find that the people's last resort will be the strongest condemnation of this project. The hon. member for Cumberland also said that the difference in the petitions which came from the east and from the west showed that there was something wrong about them. Does he not know that there were so many objections to this scheme that you could have fifteen or twenty petitions in opposition to it and if you were to put them down in ordinary sized [DOT] print you would have a petition as long as from here down to Wellington street. Does the hon. gentleman suppose that three dozen petitions could in any ordinary sized print represent all the objections that there are to this scheme, and does it not strike him, that, when the people of the west enumerate certain objections to this scheme, although they are not the same as those which the people of the east have, nevertheless, they are good objections ? Does it not also strike him that if there are so many different objections urged to this scheme by the people in the west and the people in the east there is an accumulation of evidence against it, and that there is an additional reason why the government should get more information instead of merely insulting the petitioners ? I do not know that I shall trouble the House any longer with the matter. I have said as emphatically as I can, and I wish I had language in which to say it more emphatically, that I resent and I think the people of Lincoln will resent as an insult, the words used by the right hon. Prime Minister to the effect that these

petitions are not bona fide and that therefore the government should not pay any attention, to them. The people have the right to appreciate the efforts of the opposition if they think that those efforts are well directed. What makes the government angry is that they find that not the hidebound supporters of the government but the independent Reformers so to speak as well as the Conservatives are unanimously saying that the contentions of the members of the opposition are contentions which they strongly endorse, and that they find that their party are losing strength in the country and are going to get into trouble. A few of the most important objections against this policy are set forth in these petitions. The signatories, in pursuance of their inherent right as British subjects, have petitioned the House of Commons, and asked the government to pause before the country is irrevocably committed to this scheme. Speaking as the representative of the county of Lincoln, and speaking generally of the duty of a member of this House, I say that the government should have accepted these petitions in good faith, and should have considered them in the proper spirit. If this investigation is to be made by the Privileges and Elections Committee, it must be of the widest character, and notwithstanding that the member for Brant (Mr. Heyd) has accused us of wanting free rides for. our constituents to Ottawa, I say, Sir, that the petitioners must be allowed to come before parliament and to give their evidence that they have presented these petitions in proper form.

speechtext: A little before three o'clock this afternoon the hon. member for Prince Edward (Mr. Alcorn) went to the record room, where the petitions are supposed to be kept, and asked for the two petitions to which the member for Belleclaasse referred this morning. The clerk in charge stated they were not there, and he said that the member for Bellechasse had taken them away. I want to know from the Minister of Justice or the Prime Minister, if it is proper that petitions supposed to be in charge of an officer of this House, may be peddled all over the country and left lying around on desks, and names added to them, and then have them referred to the Committee on Privileges and Elections ? These petitions are not now in the custody of the proper officers, and the members who presented them have no opportunity of seeing them. These petitions are supposed to be under lock and key, in the custody of the Clerk of this House, so that any member of this House may have access to them, but we now find that they are out of the possession of the Clerk, and presumed to be in the possession of the hon. member (Mr. Talbot) who made the charges.

The Officer who allowed thtese original petitions out of his custody should be immediately brought to the bar of
the House and punished, and some proceedings should be taken against the member for Bellechasse (Mr. Talbot) for his conduct. These are original records of parliament, and any man who takes them from the custody of the proper officer infringes on the criminal law of the country. We should have the Clerk summoned before this House, and dismissed, and we should pass upon the conduct of the man who attempted to take them from the custody of the clerk. It is an outrage, that the records of parliament should be peddled about in that way.
Amendment (Mr. Clarke) agreed to, and main motion (Mr. Talbot), ns amended.. agreed to.
Is it not necessary that there should be an Order of the House, to send these petitions before the committee ?
I think the motion provides for that. All documents of the House are always at the disposal of the members of committees, and of the members of the House also.
I am of the opinion that they should be referred to the committee by Order of the House.
I think that is provided for in the motion.

I have received a communication as to the commutation of sentence in the case of King vs. Carver. It would seem that the commutation of this sentence has provoked hostile criticism, and at the instance of my correspondent I would ask the Minister of Justice, if there is no objection, to lay upon the Table of the House the papers connected with this case. If there is any report of the judge, or any reasons assigned Tor commutation, or any petitions asking for commutation, it would be desirable, if there is to be a discussion, that these documents should be made public.

A motion has been passed in the Senate asking for the production of these papers. I have hesitated up to the present to comply with that order, because it is contrary to the practice of this House. I have a memo, made by Sir John Thompson in which he refused to produce the papers in a capital case. I am, however, considering the matter with respect to this particular case, and I will let my hon. friend know in a day or two what the decision of the judge is.
Would the decision of Sir John Thompson cover all the documents in connection with such a case ? It would not, I suppose, cover the Order in Council.
Perhaps not.

The Minister of Justice gave a memo, to ihe hon. member for Montmorency (Mr. .Casgrain) in connection with this subject, but 1 confess that I did not read it very carefully. I suppose there would be no objection to producing the documents which are not covered by any precedent. I think there was the same opinion on the part of my hon. friend (Mr. Casgrain) and myself, that these precedents did not go as far as seems to be indicated in the memo, which my hon. friend the Minister of Justice was good enough to send to us.

I would like to ask the government whether any decision lias been come to with regard to issuing the writ for St. James division, Montreal ? The matter has been brought to the attention of the House on several occasions by the hon. member for Jacques Cartier.

House again in Committee of Supply.

Why do you have the votes for dredging divided up in this way ? This is not dredging ?
No.
What is the object of this pile driving ?
The banks on these rivers have to be pro- [DOT] tected in many places, and we require the use of a pile driver.
It seems to me that it would be better if you kept the estimates for your dredges, scows, pile drivers, and all other plant separate from the estimates for the actual work done.

I think there might be an improvement in the classification. I may say that in going over these matters I found the same difficulty the hon. leader of the opposition did, and I think it would be well to have a reclassification in our estimates in that direction. It would be more convenient for this House, and still more convenient for the department.
Columbia river above Golden-opening channel from river to site of- proposed warehouse at Wilmer, $1,000.
What warehouse is this ?

Mining developments are going on there, and the products of the mines are shipped by boat. An application from Mr. Hammond, of Osier & Hammond, -who is largely interested, represents that a large amount of money has been invested in mining industries there. Therefore, I feel that this expenditure is warranted in the public interest for the purpose of improving the navigation in this river.
Is that dredging ?

This will be hand dredging.
Columbia river-improvements between Upper and Lower Arrow lakes, $12,000.

I may say that a small dredge has been
13306

built by the department and placed on this river, and this vote is for the maintenance of the dredge and its working expenses during the year.
What is the dredge doing ?
It is dredging the Columbia river. We do not require a separate item for dredging there. We own the dredge, and this is for its maintenance and operation.

Why do we vote $12,000 to maintain and operate a dredge in this place and $10,000 to maintain and operate a dredge somewhere else ? Would it not he better to have a general vote, out of which these dredges might be kept going, instead of having a separate vote for each place ?

I agree that that would be better. In this particular case the dredge is built specially. It can get neither off nor on that river. $12,000 is the total cost of the work being done. Lin I agree with my hon. friend, and if I have anything more to do with preparing the estimates, they will be prepared in that way.
Columbia river between Arrow lakes-to pay balance due on dredge machinery, $4,000.

This is a dredge that was built by the department under contract. It will cost altogether $6,000 with the machinery.
Fraser river-improvements, $25,000.
This work is done under the supervision of Mr. Keefer, the engineer of the department in the province of British Columbia.
Where is this work done?
At Nicopin island. It consists of mattrass-ing and pile-driving for the protection of the banks of the river.
Do they use the government pile-driver ?

Yes, we own all the plant there. It is all done by day labour.
Hardy Bay-wharf (revote), $2,100.

This is to complete the payment for this wharf, which was let by contract.
Quatsino city-wharf, $5,000.
This is a new vote. It is proposed to provide wharf accommodation for steamers and other vessels. This is a city in the north of Vancouver island, and it is a mining district.
How much is this work expected to cost when completed ?

The total cost is estimated at $5,000. The work will be let by contract.
Williams Head quarantine station

extension of wharf at eastern .end, &c., $5,000.
We have a government wharf there, and this is for small extensions and improvements.
Will this complete the improvements ?

That is the intention.
Victoria Harbour-additional amount for dredging and removal of rocks, $10,000.

We have both government dredges at work in that harbour, and the work was carried out very successfully. We desire to complete it, and I am informed by the engineer that this $10,000 will complete it this season.
Is this for the inner or outer harbour ?

For the inner harbour.
Public works-chargeable to income-Yukon Territory-Lewes and Yukon river improvements, $30,000.

This vote of $30,000 is proposed to apply as follows in connection with the Lewes and Yukon improvements, viz :	(a) Maintaining the training piers, dams, &c., built at the head of Lake Laberge, the object of directing the whole discharge of Lewes river into one comparatively narrow channel on the south-east side of the river which can be used by steamboats of from four to five feet draught at the lowest stage of the water ; (b) Closing the gap. of about 400 feet left in the centre of the brush and stone dam of which already 3,250 feet lineal have been built on the north-west side of the contracted artificial channel formed at the head of Lake Laberge. (c) Removing boulders from Thirty Mile river, (d) Completing some further blasting required on the rocky ledge which runs across the waterway at Five Finger rapids, in order to improve the navigable channel so as to permit of the easy and safe passage of steamboats of about four feet draught at the lowest stage of the water without having to use a cable, (e) Blasting some rock off dangerous points, &c., at the Rink rapids, (f) Improving the channel at Hellgate. (g) Increasing the depth of water over bars in the Yukon river below Selkirk and Ogilvie.
Have we a representative in this House from that section of the country ?
Yes, Mr. Chairman, we have.
Will this wol'k he done by contract ?
This work is being carried out under the .advice of the local council at Dawson city.
Municipal council or the government council ?
The government council.

I regret that, because we have an experience of that "body already, as I understand. It will be remembered Mr. Chairman, that it cost $50,000 merely to plug a hole in that country. If this money is to be expended by the same people as had control of that work, I do not think the method is a good one. It seems to me it would be better and more satisfactory if the matter were under the control of the department.
