We found it would cost more to maintain a staff of engineers in that country such as would be necessary for these works than to carry out the works under the advice of the council. That council are coming in -contact with the representatives and the shipping interest, and so have the best means of learning how the money can be most advantageously spent in the public interest in improving navigation. My hon. friend (Mr. Thomson, Grey) will admit that there are none who know more of the situation than the representatives of the shipping interest, and none who are more anxious that the work should be properly done. Since the present system was adopted, we find we get much greater value for the money expended than before. Of course, we have an engineer representing the department, who reports on these works..
I did not hear the whole of the minister's explanation, and may have misunderstood. Did he say that this money was spent by the transportation companies ?
I said the money was expended under the advice of .the Yukon council.
This is in addition to the amount placed at the disposal of the council itself ?
Yes, with this feature-that they make a report to us, and the accounts are sent here and we pay them.
Who initials the accounts ?

The accountant of the Yukon.
*fu ^
In keeping the accounts, would this amount be included in the expenditure of the territory ?

It is entirely under the charge of the Public Works Department here. The hon. gentleman will remember that I mentioned seven or eight points at which improvements were to be made, and I explained that the work could be done more efficiently and cheaply than by maintaining our own engineers in that country.
Can they carry out the work and charge what they like, or does the department's engineer there employ the men ?

They make a report to the department-and we scrutinize the accounts. But they employ the men to carry out the work.
Harbours and rivers generally, $3,500.
What is this for ?
This is the usual vote.
What can be done with this small item ? What kind of improvements can be carried on with this ?
It is for contingencies and different small accounts. It has been voted annually for a long time.

It always seemed to me that the voting of these small general amounts is absurd. We have accounts for each locality for dredging, and then a general account ; accounts for repairs to dredges, and a general account. And here we have another of these small Items. I suppose this $35,000 applies to the whole Dominion, and can be used anywhere. But what can be done with an amount like this I cannot understand.
The 'MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. It is because we take special votes for dredging here and there, instead of having one vote, which I think would be better, that a general item like this is needed. There are incidental expenses in connection with all the works-stationery and other contingencies-to be met out of this general item.
I could understand a vote of some size, but I cannot see what is the use of voting $3,500.
I desire to bring to the attention of the hon. minister the fact that in the year 1900 a public work was commenced in a place called Skinner's Pond, in West Prince, P.E.I.
Was it before or after the election ?
Immediately before the election. I would like to ask the minister if he intends to drop that work after having expended $2,000 on it, or does he intend to continue it ?
Will the hon. gentleman say where Skinner's Pond is?

It is just as good a name as Pile-o'-Bones creek, or any other.
I would like to ask the minister if he intends to prosecute this work at Skinner's Pond, where $2,000 have already been expended.
I have no information with regard to this matter. I do not find anything in the estimates for any work there. What kind of work was commenced there, may I ask the hon. gentleman ?

The hon. gentleman ought to .know, he has the facts before him. It -was cutting a channel through the sandbar into the land near Skinner's Pond, in a region where there are many other points on the coast of Prince Edward Island. It was supposed to be a great advantage. Now the minister has the chief engineer at his elbow, who should be able to tell us what is going to be done now that the elections are coming on.
I do not know that the chief engineer is intersted in elections. He tells me it was opening up a small channel, and was reported to give satisfaction.

Surely it is not the intention of the department, after commencing this work on the eve of the last election, to drop it immediately after the election. Is it the intention, now that another election is coming on, to go on and complete the work ?
I have no knowledge whatever. The chief engineer says $2,000 was spent there.
Do I understand the minister to say that he will make further inquiries ?
I will be pleased to give instructions to have the local engineer make a report with regard to this work.
I think this item better stand until we get full information.

Yes, let it stand.
Item allowed to stand.
Dredging-including salaries of engineers, superintendents and clerks. Dredging-Maritime provinces-additional amount required, $28,500.
This is an additional amount required for carrying on dredging operations in the maritime provinces.

In the moneys provided for public works in the maritime provinces, I notice that there are no items
under the head of dredging alone, but they are all for the construction or repair of dredges. It seems strange that this item should be in the former class.
It is a general statement as to how the money is to be used.

I think it would be better to place it under the head of rivers and harbours generally than to place it where money is required for building and repairing dredges. It is not a proper classification. Every other item is for the construction of dredges, here it is for dredging, a different matter altogether.
I do not know that the department is responsible for this classification.
The amount of money that is appropriated for improvements in the maritime provinces is so large that a portion of it had better be under some other head.

We send the items over to the department, and when they are printed we find them in this way. I imagine that is being done with the items of the other departments. There is no intention to cover up anything. That money cannot be used for any other purpose than dredging in the maritime provinces. .
Could the minister tell me what dredging has been done in the province of Prince Edward Island in connection with this vote ?
If the hon. member will wait till that item comes up in the estimates, I will give him a list of what is being done there, or I will give him the information now.
What has been done at Cape Tormentine and Pointe du Ch6ne in regard to dredging ?
No dredging has been done at Cape Tormentine this year. The dredging at Pointe du Chene was completed early this season and the dredge left there some months ago.
At about what time ?

Some time in July the work was completed.
air. HACKETT. Where was the work done at that particular place ?
Along the base of the pier.
What depth of water is there now and what space has been dredged ?
About seventeen feet at low water.
What space ?

I cannot remember the figures sufficiently well to give my hon. friend correct information, but I will be very glad to bring down a report showing the hon. gentleman just what space has been dredged.
New dredging plant, British Columbia, to replace snag boat 'Samson' and dredge 'Mud Lark,' $10,000.
Are these out of service or what has become of them ?

This is the commencement of a somewhat important vote. The snag boat has become unfit for use, worn out and the ' Mud Lark' is in the same position. They have been doing some work but they have been reported ns being unfit for work, and it is desirable that we should renew the plant. The new snag boat is estimated to cost $20,000 and the dredge to replace the ' Mud Lark ' $30,000.
This is the first vote ?
This is the first vote in an expenditure of some $50,000.
Will a contract be let by tender ?
Yes.
Where is it proposed to build this new snag boat and dredge ?
They are generally built on the const. They have been built in the past by companies from Toronto or Montreal.
What about the ' Samson ' and ' Slud Lark ' ?

They are generally disposed of by public advertisement.
New tug for dredge ' Manitoba,' $10,500.
Is this for the province of SInnitoba ?
This is the total cost of the new tug required.
Where is it to bo placed ?
On Lake SInnitoba. This is an entirely new tug. a strong one and more competent to do the work that is required of it.
Was there a vote last year for the construction or purchase of a new dredge for that province ?
Yes, the chief engineer informs me that there was a vote last year and that a dredge was purchased.
There is no item for dredging at the mouth of Slossy river. I noticed that there was a vote last year. Has that work been finished ?
I put the item in the main estimates.
Has any work been done there yet ?
No.
Is it going to be done this year ? There is a large sandbar which prevents boats coming in and going out at low water and this work is very necessary.

The chief engineer informs me that it is difficult 'to get the dredge up. It was the intention to take it up during high water. It cannot be got up at all times. Perhaps the hon. gentleman will know that is the reason why the work was not carried out for which a sum was voted last year.
Hydraulic self-propelling dredge for maritime provinces, $40,000.
What is the name of this dredge ?
It has not been christened yet. This is a vote of $40,000 for the purpose of building a new self-propelling dredge for the maritime provinces.
What is the total cost ?

I think the hon. members of this committee will agree with me that we require some better plant for spending the money that we have voted. We have voted money for dredging at important points from year to year and no work has been done. We either should not vote the money or else we should have some good plant to carry out the work in a satisfactory manner. There are several important harbours in the maritime provinces where we have no plant to do the work. Some of the dredges that we have are small and could not do the work at these harbours. The intention is to build or purchase a new plant. The total cost will be about $120,000.
What will be the capacity of the dredge ?
This is a suction dredge with a capacity of about 1,000 yards an hour.
Who is the builder and how is it to be built ?
We will have to advertise for tenders. It will be built by contract.

I entirely agree with the government's policy in construct-

ing these dredges. The only thing X regret is that there are not more public moneys appropriated for a similar purpose. I am satisfied that if the government owned more dredges and did the work themselves the work would be done for one-half what it costs now by letting it to outsiders who have dredges for this purpose. I am confident that it will meet with the approval of the country.
Might I ask the hon. minister where this new dredge will be constructed and what will be the total cost ?

Specifications will be prepared in the department for the kind of dredge that we want and we will advertise for tenders.
New dredge for Prince Edward Island, $25,000.
The old dredge in Prince Edward Island is very unsatisfactory. The expectation is that we can have a dredge to do satisfactory work in Prince Edward Island at a total cost of $25,000.

It is quite impossible that you can get a dredge to do the work around Prince Edward Island for $25,000. The old dredge was taken over from the local government at confederation ; it is thirty years old, and it originally cost over $40,000. It is a small thing for the government of Canada to propose to replace her by a dredge that will only cost $25,000.

I am informed by the engineer that you can build a better dredge now for $25,000 than you could for $40,000 when the old one was built. The engineer has some experience, and he knows that my instructions are to give the House full information so far as he can as to the cost of these things. I may say to the hon. gentleman (Mr. Hackett) that the first cost of the old dredge was about $23,500.
She cost $40,000.
How will this work be done ?
Tenders will be advertised for.
May I ask the minister if any dredges are being built at Sorel ?
I am informed that they have more work on hand at Sorel than they can attend to.

What are they doing ?
The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS. They are building two or three large dredges and scows, &c.

I may say that $25,000 will build a splendid dredge, as good a dredge as we have on the upper lakes, and she is a very good one having a capacity of from 800 to 1,000 yards daily.
In the main estimates, on page 55, there is a vote of $5,000 for harbours and rivers generally, and in the supplementaries there is a vote of $3,500 for the same purpose. That is additional to the amount In the main estimates ?
Yes.
In the main estimates you have an item : ' New dredging plant, maritime provinces ; new hydraulic dredge, $200,000.'
That is a different kind of dredge altogether ; that is for the * W. S. Fielding ' that is being built at Sorel.
Is the material for these dredges obtained by public tender ?
So far as I know, yes.
Will this dredge lie built in Prince Edward Island ?

We will have to build her wherever the most satisfactory tender comes from. I dare say that the contract for the hull may be in Prince Edward Island, and the contract for the machinery might toe separate, or the contractor for the hull might buy the machinery, according to specifications, from the different manufacturers.
How many dredges have you at the present time ?
The deputy thinks we have 19.
How many under construction ?
One.
How long before this dredge for Prince Edward Island will be completed ?

We will advertise at once for tenders, and there is no reason why it should not be completed during the next season. There are urgent demands for dredging from different parts of the Dominion, and I believe that this dredging work is necessary for the improvement of our harbours and the development of the trade of the country. We wish to secure this plant at the earliest possible moment. We have made inquiries with regard to purchasing plant, but we have had no suitable offers, or I would be quite willing to accept them. We want a first-class, up-to-date plant that will give satisfaction. As soon as this vote is passed we will advertise for tenders for the Prince Edward Island dredge.
When the minister says that he will advertise, he means in the public press of the country ?
Yes.

As there are so many dredges now under construction, I would ask the Minister of Public Works to make a red mark on the wall with respect to my appeal for dredging to be done in the county of Lunenburg.	.

I may say that the appeal of the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kaulbach) is one of the principal reasons which has convinced me as to the necessity of getting more dredging plant. We have no dredge at the present time that [DOT]can satisfactorily do that work.

I will look forward with a very great deal of expectation and hope that this appeal of mine, which I have made so frequently, will be acceded to at the earliest possible moment. I hope it will be the first appeal attended to.

I would not like to make any rash promise that it will be the first, but I will see how the hon. gentleman (Mr. Kaulbach) behaves 'himself. However, seriously speaking, that is the intention, and this is one of the most important works that we want this new plant for.

From the amount of money voted for dredging in the maritime provinces, I do not see why our hon. friend from Lunenburg (Mr. Kaulbach) should not have all the dredging he requires in his constituency. I find in the main estimates, at page 55, tha,t $87,000 is voted for dredging in Nova Scotia, Prince Edward Island and New Brunswick, and in these supplementary estimates $28,500 more is voted. These amounts far exceed the amounts voted for the upper provinces, so that I think the hon. member for Lunenburg should have the dredging he wants done in his constituency to his entire satisfaction.

If my hon. friend from North Grey (Mr. Thomson) looks more closely, he will find a special vote for dredging in the hon. gentleman's constituency ; but, as I have explained, no matter how much money we vote, we have not any dredge to do the work.
'Mr. KAULBACH. 1 may inform the hon. Minister of Public Works that I shall be satisfied with the dredge he has on hand at present until he Can get a superior one, and then of course we shall expect to have the remainder of the work completed.

I am perfectly willing to make a bargain with my hon. friend; but the chief engineer of the department and the hon. gentleman between them decided that the dredge could not do the work, and therefore if I sent it there, it would not be very satisfactory.

The harbours in the constituency of Halifax have not been dredged for three or four years, and we have been waiting with a good deal of patience until a dredge could be procured. There are a number of harbours in that county which are suffering because the dredges are occupied elsewhere. But I would point out to the hon. minister that before any promise is made to the outlying counties of Nova Scotia, he should remember that the promise has been made for some time that the harbours of Halifax county would be attended to, and the people of that county would be unwilling to see any outlying counties take precedence. I would like to have this impressed on the hon. Minister of Public Works.
I wish to emphasize the statement in regard to the fishermen which has just emanated from my hon. friend who has just taken his seat ; because no better class can be found anywhere.
Is it a fact that the hon. junior member for Halifax (Mr. Roche) has made the statement here that the fishermen live on the outskirts of civilization ? Is that true ?

About as true as a great many of the statements made on the other side of the House-made out of whole cloth. I never stated any -such thing. I may have stated that they lived on the extreme verge of the country, that is, nearest the ocean, but if anybody thinks the fisherman is a greenhorn or is outside the limits of civilization, he makes a great mistake. Mistakes of that kind will arise in Ontario ; that is where half truths emanate from ; but they do not emanate from the member for Halifax. I wish the hon. gentleman to understand that I am not in the habit of making rash statements of that kind. What I do say I am quite willing to stand by on every occasion. I never disparge any one,

either friend or foe. I am not such an idiot as to do that.

Will my hon. friend tell us what he did say V
Mr. ItOCHE (Halifax). It is in ' Hansard.'
I do not wish to make a statement which I can corroborate or supp jrt, and I have here the words of the hon. gentleman as he uttered them-that the fishermen of Nova Scotia
What page ?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must draw the attention of the hon. member to the fact that he cannot read from a former debate.

I am not reading. I am simply stating the words of the hon. gentleman as he uttered them, that the fishermen of Nova Scotia lived on the outskirts of civilization. I simply took down the words of the hon. gentleman as he uttered them, and I repudiate the statement.
Is the hon. gentleman quoting from ' Hansard.' If so, from what page ?

The hon. gentleman is very desirous of having pages, but, I am quoting his words exactly as he uttered them. Now, I resent that on the part of the fishermen of Nova Scotia.
pretation he pleases upon his own remarks in regard to people in his own locality. There is no resemblance whatever between the fishermen in the hon. gentleman's constituency and the fishermen in my constituency.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must draw the attention of the hon. member to the fact that this discussion is out of order.
New dredging plant, British Columbia-one tug, steel hull, and two hopper scows, $36,000.

Here is another illustration of what I- spoke about. Just a little above, you have another item for dredging plant at British Columbia, $10,000. Why not put all the dredging plant in one item in each province, so that we may know how much is spent in each province.
I agree with the hon. gentleman and I am sorry these items are entered in this way. It is inconvenient for me, and I would prefer to have them altogether.

What is the estimated cost ?
. The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS. The tug will cost $20,000 and the two steel hopper scows $8,000 each.
Will they be built in British Columbia ?

I rise to a point of order. The hon. member for West Prince (Mr. Hackett) has attributed certain observations to the hon. junior member for Halifax, who has denied having uttered them. I submit that in view of the fact that the hon. gentleman is not prepared to state the authority from which lie quotes, he has to accept the denial of the hon. member for Halifax.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The rule is quite clear. When a certain statement is attributed to an hon. member, and when the hon. member says he did not make any such statement, then the whole thing has to cease. The statement of the hon. member who has been charged must be accepted in good faith.

Will; you permit me, Mr. Chairman, to repel any such insinuation with regard to the fishermen of the province from which I come. They are not living on the outskirts of civilization, but they are well-to-do citizens, who earn more money than the average merchant or professional man or farmer, and they are as respectable a class of people as we have in Ontario. To say that these people live on the outskirts of civilization, or that they are not as competent to do business as the rest of our people, is something that I must repudiate.
If the hon. gentleman wishes to make remarks, he is at perfect liberty to do so ; he may put any inter-417*

If there are any firms in British Columbia able to do this class of work and I understand there are-they will be given an opportunity to tender.
New dredging plant, Ontario and-Quebec-additional amount, $78,000.

In the main estimates we asked for a vote of $75,000 for new dredging plant for Ontario and Quebec. That is the way moneys have been voted since confederation for this dredging plant. We purchased the ' International ' plant, a large steam dredge and scows belonging to Mr. Connolly the contractor. This plant cost originally, $180,000. There was a dispute between the Connollys and the government when this plant was offered for sale, and I asked Mr. Stevens, one of the most competent men in the service at Halifax, to examine and report on the plant. On his report and that of Mr. Howden of the department, we concluded that it was a good purchase and that by purchasing it we would save two years, which it would take us to procure a plant at all equal to this in order to carry on the works for which money was voted. The whole purchase price was $123,000.
What was included in the purchase ?

I have not the particulars, but speaking generally it includes a dredge, a good tug,

four scows, all the duplicates, &c. I am satisfied that the department has now a first-class deep water dredging plant.
What is the capacity of ' the dredge ?
About 6,000 yards per day. It was built at Kingston, Ontario, in 1894. It has a steel hull.
Where is this dredge to be used ?
At all the deep water points in the province of Quebec, down in the St. Lawrence. This plant may be used in salt water and will dredge anywhere from fifteen to sixty feet.
Was this dredge purchased after examination and estimate as to value ?

The first thing I did was to get Mr. Stevens of the Marine Department, who was reported to me as the most competent man in the Dominion to examine machinery of that kind, to examine it. Then we have the report of the officers of our own department, especially Mr. Howden, who has been in the service some twenty-five or thirty years in connection with this work, and who is said to be a man of very high character and a very efficient judge. From the reports of these men we decided to make the purchase.
Mr. Stevens, the government inspector of machinery in Nova Scotia, is one of the most competent men in Nova Scotia.
Will the minister bring down these reports ?
Yes, I will have them brought down and lay them on the Table.
Then, it is understood that we can discuss this item further.
Certainly.
May I ask to go back to the item for the hydraulic dredge in the maritime provinces ? I would like to know what is the character and capacity of that dredge ?
The capacity will be about 1,000 yards per hour.
Will this $40,000 cover the cost ?
Oh, no. The chief engineer estimate's the cost at $120,000.	-
Is anything included in that estimate besides the dredge proper ?
No.	I
In what 'depth of water will this dredge be able to work ?
As deep as thirty or thirty-five feet.
In how shallow water can she work ?
She is a suction dredge ; she will have a draught of about five feet, and can work in about eight feet of water.
If only $40,000 is voted and the total cost will be $120,000, I am afraid we can scarcely expect to see that dredge in operation next year. At what time is it expected to be available for use ?

I cannot say definitely. Of course, I could not procure the plans until I had the authority of parliament. I am making all the speed I can, and, so far as the department is concerned, there will be no delay that can possibly be avoided.

I suppose there is no intention of proceeding next year with making the channel by the Canadian route between Gananoque and Brockville. I understand the government rnadfe a complete survey of that channel. There is not so much dredging to be done.
I do not intend to proceed this season. I have not taken any special vote for the improvement of that channel.

I might suggest to the hon. Minister of Public Works that some time, when he is taking a trip up the river St. Lawrence, he might take a look at a rock or shoal in the narrows at Brockville. I brought the matter to the attention of the minister two or three years ago, and a buoy was placed there but the channel is very narrow, and buoying does not obviate the difficulty. It is merely a large rock, I should say, lying tlieTe in eight or nine feet of water, and I think it would not take very much money to clear that obstruction and make a first-class channel through the narrows. The American government have removed all obstructions on their side of the channel, so that, on the route between Cape Vincent and Ogdensburg, this is the only real obstruction that might cause accident. It is only three or four years since a large steamer with her consort struck this rock, and very great loss resulted. I mention the matter so that the minister might kindly look at it and see if it would not be possible to have this obstruction removed.

Some day, when the hon. gentleman (Mr. Reid, Grenville) has his yacht out, I shall be glad to accept his invitation and take this trip. But the,survey ha* been made, and the engineer has the plans in the department, and an estimate is being made up which I

shall be prepared to submit to my hon. friend.
Roads and bridges ' Hull slide ' union bridges and roadway approaches-repairs, alerations and additions, &e., $6,000.

This is to replace sidewalks, roadway and approaches destroyed in the great Hull and pttiiwa fire. The total cost of the work is estimated at $12,800.
Ottawa city-Dufferin and Sappers bridges over the Rideau canal-repairs, alterations and additions, $10,000.
I thought this work was finished.

This is to cover the cost of road, sidewalk and approaches, granolithic or asphalt, including, if necessary, iron girders. This work is being done on the recommendation of the officers of the department and will cost $15,600.
There was a considerable expenditure on these bridges, and I thought we were done with them for a considerable length of time ; but the work is hardly finished before we commence again.
That is exactly how the matter struck me, but I am informed that the work done was merely temporary work. But the work is to be' done now in a first-class and permanent manner.

When it is considered that nearly all the traffic between west and east in the city of Ottawa passes over these two bridges, it will be seen that the work is necessary. But I question if the minister can carry out the necessary repairs and improvements for this amount.
Is this an iron bridge ?

Yes.
Bryson bridge-reconstruction of piers and approaches, $10,000.
This is over the Ottawa river at Bryson.
Is this an interprovincial bridge ?
Yes, it is a wagon bridge across Calumet Island in the river. There are two bridges. I think, one from the Quebec side and one from the Ontario side.
Does the government build wagon bridges ?
They must have built this one.

Then we are doing a work that belongs to the Quebec
government. I think the minister bad better look into this.

I know that the bridge is government property. Representations have been made to the department about it, and I inquired why the Dominion government had built the bridge. I have made arrangements with the county that they are to take possession of the bridge and relieve the Dominion of any further expense in regard to this matter, and this vote was given upon that condition. It is for renewing a bridge built there some years ago. The total cost of the bridge was $15,500. It is a steel bridge, but it was built on wooden piers that have become undermined.
I thiulc that belongs to the province of Quebec; that island is entirely within that province.

1 think that probably it is a provincial work, legally. But the government did some years ago build this bridge, and are responsible for it. We are to put it into good shape, and the county is to maintain it hereafter.
This other bridge at Ottawa, the union bridge, is that an interprovincial bridge ?	*
I am not very well posted. It is government property and we get considerable revenue.

I am speaking of the interprovincial bridge between Quebec and Ontario at Hull. Has it any connection with what is called the slides that are in the city of Hull and belong to the province of Quebec ?

No the slides are Dominion property. There are two bridges over the slides that are Dominion works, and we maintain them.
Moisie Post road-improvement of, $700.

This is to keep up a road in connection with our Dominion telegraph lines along the north shore of the St. Lawrence, for a distance of about 300 miles. There have been improvements made from time to time in order to carry on the telegraphic work, to remove obstructions in order to enable material to be carried across a rough country.
It is the duty of the province to keep up that road. The government is not taking any grants to build a roadway along the Yukon telegraph line, and why do you build a road down there ?
This line was built in 1886. It runs from the east shore of the Saguenay along the shore of the St. Lawrence river down to Belle Isle.
Then the item ought to be under the head of telegraph lines.

I agree with the hon. gentleman, so far as my judgment goes. It is ridiculous to say that this is for the Moisie road. It is a vote for the maintenance of telegraph lines. I heg to move that the words * Moise post road' be struck out and that the words ' North Shore Telegraph Line ' be inserted in lieu thereof.

Motion agreed to.
Edmonton bridge over the Saskatchewan river -renewal of flooring, $1,650.

["I agree with the hon. gentleman, so far as my judgment goes. It is ridiculous to say that this is for the Moisie road. It is a vote for the maintenance of telegraph lines. I heg to move that the words * Moise post road' be struck out and that the words ' North Shore Telegraph Line ' be inserted in lieu thereof."]

Trains and teams have to cross over this bridge on the same level as it is both a railway and wagon bridge. It is not wide enough for the two, aud I think that the traffic in the near future will require that an additional bridge shall be constructed or an enlargement of the present bridge at one side or the other for the use of teams shall be made. I took the liberty once before of pointing out to the hon. minister, that, wherever a railway bridge across a stream or river in the Northwest Territories is constructed, beside or under the railway track there should be a wagon road. I am satisfied that it would be of incalculable benefit to settlers if that should be brought about. There should be a separate wagon road instead of having the wagon road and the railroad together.
The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS. The matter has been brought to the attention of the department and the engineer is looking into it.
To open a pack trail from Peace river to Pelly river $25,000.
The MINISTER OB' PUBLIC WORKS. At the request of the Department of the Interior it is proposed to open a pack trail 650 miles long from the Peace River landing to the head-waters of the Pelly river.

There was a good deal of money expended and of course it had to be expended in haste at the time of the Yukon excitement in building the Atha-baska trail to Peace River landing. They took that trail over the worst possible route that could have been selected for a trail. It is not necessary as a matter of fact to have a trail into that part of the country as yet, because the water-ways are available and one can get to Peace River landing much more readily by water than by land, but in case the trail is constructed it should be kept more to the west than when the old Athabasca trail was constructed. In building the trail through the Peace River valley by the route proposed, it will be found to be a very difficult one. Yrou would find1 it as easy to follow the Liard river route rather than the route which has been outlined. I think you will find it necessary to construct the old Athabasca Landing trail Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
to Peace River over again, as it has all grown up and is almost impassable.
Who is going to do this work and how is it going to be done ?

The former work was done by the officers of the North-west Territories. I dare say that probably the best way this money can be expended is to expend it under the direction of the officers of the government of the North-west Territories.
Under the officers of the government of the North-west Territories ?
The district is far away and inaccessible and these people are interested in getting value out of the money.
You mean the North-west council ?
Yes.

I may say in regard to the last trail constructed that the money was very well expended. A young officer named Chalmers, who was afterwards shot in South Africa, had charge of the work on the frail. He gave very careful supervision to the work and did it excellently.

I am not objecting at all to the way in which the work was done, and I am not saying that it was inefficiently done, but we have been voting a great many items for the North-west Territories, and I would like at some time during the passage of these estimates if the hon. minister could give us the various items together with the aggregate amount that we have voted for this purpose.
This is practically a grant to the Northwest Territories.

We have passed several items of this kind already. Then, there is another thing. Do these gentlemen in the North-west Territories receive pay for doing this work? They get their salaries as they are under contract to do police work. Do they get extra for this work ?
No, they receive no extra pay. The officers to whom I referred are the officers of the North-west council.

I think I may have misled my hon. friend (Mr. Sproule). This officer had been formerly in the police, but I do not think he was an officer of the police at the time he took charge of this work for the North-west council.
This will be done by the North-west Council ?

This is a long way from Ottawa, and we have to consider the best way to get value

for the money. The North-west Council are extremely Interested to satisfy the people that they should get the most value for this money, and they will do the work and send vouchers, properly certified, here. They have men of special experience for this kind of work.	[DOT]

I do not object to that.
I heard a rumour that Mr. Charleson was to go out there to do this work, and I do not think that the country requires a second experience in the near future of the manner in which he expends money. I assume that the North-west Council will make every dollar go as far as it can, but if it were to be spent by some commission sent out, Including Mr. Charleson, I certainly would object to it.
Assistance towards extension of telephone line from Chatham to Tracadie, N.B., $2,000.
This is a grant we are giving to a private company to connect a line with the Lazaretto.
Do you get any return for this grant ?
The deputy tells me that we have not made any contract, but I suppose there will be a condition as to certain government messages going free.
You ought to have that understood beforehand. If the money is voted, the company is likely to try and get out of any bargain of that kind.

I agree with my hon. friend, but this is a small matter, and I think we may leave it with the deputy minister to arrange proper terms.
Telegraphic connection between Deer Island and Eastport, Me., $3,503.
This is an extension of our own line for 10 miles.
Doees it cost $350 a mile ?

There are two miles of cable which will cost $1,200, and the cost of the land line is $110 a mile.
Anticosti Island-renewal of line wire between Fox Bay and Bescie river, $7,360.
This is for a renewal of 60 miles of our present line.
What stations have tlie government on Anticosti ?

There are seven stations.
To pay for Marconi wireless telegraph apparatus at Chateau Bay and Belle Isle, $4,100.
What success has attended this Marconi system ?
The report of the officer in charge is that since July this station has been working very satisfactorily. This line extends for 22 miles.
Have we not a station for ocean telegraphic purposes ?
This station is not used for communicating with ships as yet, but it can be so used.
We voted $80,000 last year for the Marconi system.
That was for erecting a station at Glace Bay.
Yes ; and we see it announced in the press, from time to time, that the system has been a success and so on. Can the minister give us any information about that 1
The arrangements in that regard have been carried out by the Department of Finance, and my hon. friend will be able to get the information when the Minister of Finance comes into the Chamber.

Could not this station be made to work for outgoing or incoming vessels ? If we had had a station there somewhat similar to what they have in New York, it might possibly have prevented some of the accidents which have happened, and perhaps some of the large steamers now going to Montreal which have not the system on board would adopt it.

We have an expert in the department who is at the head of the telegraphic business, and I will endeavour to obtain any information which he may have on this subject.
Telegraph line-Murray Bay to St. Catherines Bay. second wire, $1,640.
This is for a second wire on our own line betw'een these two points.
What is the distance between these points ?
Forty-one miles.

Might I ask what the hon. gentleman is doing to establish a telegraphic service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland ? It is a matter that has been brought up frequently, and the minister said he would consider it ; and I trust that he will see his way clear to place an amount in the estimates to wipe away what is called a monopoly down there.

My hon. friend knows that some arrangement was made with the company which has the telegraphic system between the is-

land and the mainland, and the Dominion granted it a subsidy. Legal questions have arisen, however, and if the hon. gentleman would take my advice, he would ask us to cancel the subsidy until the company afforded a satisfactory service. With the improvements in wireless telegraphy, we may be able to establish a couple of Marconi stations on the island, and in that way do away with this monopoly.
Does the government control the rates ?
No, I think the arrangement was made between the Island government and the company previous to confederation.

That is correct. I insist on having some answer from the government in this regard. Some years ago we were told by Sir Louis H. Davies, who was then a member of the government, that there was no monopoly, and since then nothing has been done. The people of Prince Edward Island are insisting on this accommodation every year, and I, as one of their representatives, stand here again to insist on having justice done to the island. We find in these estimates a vote of $3,500 for telegraphic communication between Deer island and Eastport, Maine, while nothing has been done for the people of Prince Edward Island. I would ask the minister seriously to consider the conditions that now exist, and to do something in the near future to relieve the people of that province from the incubus of this monopoly, which has weighed so heavily upon them for the last fifty years.

1 am not going to express any opinion; but 1 shall be pleased to do anything I can to help my hon. friend. If the people of the island would take my advice, I think they would get better arrangements with the company. If not, I suppose parliament would have power to bring in legislation to remove the monopoly.

There is a great opportunity now, to meet the wishes of the hon. gentleman and the people of the island. We have just passed a grant to aid a press cable service, and I understood, when that matter was discussed, that the Minister of Finance promised to see that the papers on the island should have the benefit of the service as well as the papers on the mainland.
I have no doubt that there will be a discussion on this matter when the question of the cable service comes up.
Can the minister give any idea of what revenue he expects from these lines ?
I do not know that I can ; but the revenue is very small.
It is not equal to the amount spent annually in keeping them in repair ?

No, nothing like it ; but a large number of people are benefited by it.
Mr. REID (Grenville)'. About $40,000 is spent annually in keeping these lines in repair, and there appears to be less than $20,000 per annum of revenue ?

Having made a little inquiry the other day, l am pleased to be able to tell my hon. friend that I find that our revenue in the North-west from these lines more than doubled last year ; so that in course of time it may be that with the development of the country, we shall obtain a revenue that will pay for the service.
Is the hon. Minister of Justice in his seat ?
No.
I would like to have his opinion, and have it made public, whether the Anglo-American Company have a right to monopolize the telegraphic system between Prince Edward Island and the mainland ?
There will be a vote on which this matter will come up for discussion, when the Minister of Justice will be present, and when lie will be able to give my hon. friend more information than I can.
Would it cost much to establish some stations under the Marconi system on the island, to compete with this monopoly which my hon. friend speaks of ?
I think the wireless telegraphic system at the present time is somewhat expensive; but the result might be good in the end.

The great difficulty is that the government tell us from time to time that they are going to do better next time. If they cannot break up this monopoly, I would ask them to institute the Marconi system.

Would the govern-men have any objection to placing a telephone service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland ? If this monopoly cannot be interfered with by the government, perhaps the hon. member would approve of a telephone service.

I would be only too pleased to vote for any competition, whether by telephone or by the Marconi system or by any other method, which would relieve our people from this monopoly. We are a small population, about 20,000 people, but we are up to date.
You are not on the confines of civilization.

No, we are right in the centre of civilization, and I would ask the government to insist on a telegraph service being given us which would satisfy the people and. do away with the necessity of our complaining every year to parliament. There is not an hon. gentleman in any of the other provinces who does not desire to see justice done to this small sister province, and I am certain that I will have the support of hon. gentlemen from the other provinces in insisting on proper telegraphic communication being afforded us.	.

It would seem a desirable place for testing the Marconi system. That system is being worked to the Magdalen islands, some twenty-three or twenty-five miles distance, and surely it could be worked easily to Prince Edward Island. It is not a very costly system to install and this will be a splendid place to try it.
I am very much surprised that hon. members from Prince Edward Island sitting opposite have not raised their voice in favour of the island.

That matter is not before the House at present. If the hon. gentleman had been in parliament as long as I have, he would have heard this question discussed over and over again by lion, members on both sides. It is a legal question to a very great extent. The hon. member for Grey (Mr. Thomson) made a very pertinent question with regard to the Marconi system, but to discuss the contract and the subsidy is now out of order.
But I am talking of a telephone service.
A discussion on the telegraphic system of the island is out of order.

I am appealing on behalf of the island to have a telephone system installed between it and the mainland.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS Will the hon. gentleman tell me whether or not under the contract between the island and this company, this government could install a telephone service between the island and the mainland ?

I say it can. At the time of confederation a telephone system was not thought of. If the hon. minister J would bring in a vote to install a telephone j system between the island and the main-, land. I am satisfied that even hon. members in the opposition would support it.
The MINISTER OF PUBLIC WORKS All the lawyers put a different construction on the contract.
I would recommend the government to lay a cable across.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
We are not discussing a contract between a certain company and Prince Edward Island or the advisability of establishing any line between the mainland and Prince Edward Island.
I would ask the committee to come back to the point.
Are not the committee in order in discussing this item and comparing the telegraphic facilities on the island with those in other parts of the country ?
Supposing that could be brought under discussion, it would be far better to bring it up when the proper estimates are under consideration, and we have the proper officials here.
I desire' to insist on the rights of Prince Edward Island.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Any discussion with regard to the facilities which Prince Edward Island has now for telegraphic service is entirely out of order. This question will come up under the heading of the Finance Department and it will then be in order to discuss it.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.
Bill (No. 264) respecting the Ottawa Valley Railway Company.-Mr. Etbier.
House again in Committee of Supply.
['1 will give that information on the Yukon vote. Mr. Chairman, we have done a little work at any rate, and perhaps we had better rise.\nSome resolutions reported.']
May I ask the necessity for this second wire from Murray Bay to St. Catherine's Bay ?

In 1902 the Great North-western Telegraph Company laid a special wire from Quebec to Murray Bay to afford better connection with the North Shore Line. The second wire of the government is provided with the same idea, and so supply local offices. Generally, I may say, it is to improve the telegraph communication between these two points.
Telegraph lines-Quebec-Island of Orleans, land line, extension to Ste. Famille, $1,150.
This is an extension of seven miles, and the vote is estimated to cover the cost.
Has any explanation been given on any previous item as to the working of the Marconi Telegraph System ?

Yes, there was considerable discussion on that point. I suggested that the general discussion on the Marconi System would be more in order when the estimates of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) are under consideration, and as he is more familiar with the matter, nil communications with respect to it having taken place under his department.

As I pointed out last session, there is this observation to make, that if the system is capable of being worked at all it should be capable of being utilized for certain short distances around our own coasts. As we have granted some assistance, it seems to me the government should be in a position to give some definite information as to the prospects of making it successful along our own coast.

My hon. friend was not present when we had a discussion on this item. I read a paragraph from the report of the engineer a short time ago showing that the line from the coast to Ste. Famille had been working very satisfactorily. That is about all the information I could give.
Land line-Ste. Anne du Saguenay, to Des-cente des Femmes, $1,500.
This line is 22 miles long. The total cost will be $2,640.
Are these lines solely for the purpose of the government, or are they open for use by private individuals ?

They are used as a regular public line. The revenue in this district is about 50 per cent of the cost. That district is settling up very well in some parts, and the settlers require more means of communication.

What is the principle adopted by the government in the construction of these lines ? Do they construct them only in cases where the government require the service, or do they construct them in cases where the public may be served as well as the government ?

There have been some cases which covered both principles. I imagine some of these extensions have been made where the government had no particular use for them, and they were made chiefly for the public.

That means that we have in some portions of the country a government system of telegraphs, not more for the requirements of the government than for the people at large. Is the hon. gentleman in a position to say how many miles of telegraph lines of that kind we have ?
I think we have 5,720 miles under government control.

Before recess we were discussing the telegraph line connecting Prince Edward Island with the rest of the Dominion of Canada, and I asked the Minister of Justice if he would give his opinion regarding an alleged monopoly in connection with that telegraph line.

A gentleman interested in the telegraph company recently prepared a statement which was submitted to the Prime Minister and by him forwarded to the Department of Justice, in which I understand they claim that they have got some monopoly or some privileges which are being interfered with by legislation passed during the present session of parliament. I have not had an opportunity of looking into the memorial, and do not intend to until after the session. But so far as this parliament is concerned, we have hitherto proceeded on the assumption that there is no monopoly.
Telegraph line on north shore of St. Lawrence-land line from Bersimis to Godbout, $12,000.

This is to make provision for substituting an all-land line, about 80 miles in length, for the present cable connection between these two points. The cable seems to be always out of order and is very unsatisfactory.
Would the hon. gentleman explain the necessity for this work V
The cable has been down about seventeen or eighteen years and is completely used up, and is now useless.

Bersimis and Godbout are two important stations on the north shore of the St. Lawrence below Tadousac. There are on that coast several indentations and deep bays. Instead of building the line originally around these bays, they extended it across through the water, laying cables for the purpose. I understand that these cables have been very much interfered with by ice in spring and by the tempests, and the proposal now is to lay a land line in substitution for these cables around the bays rather than across them.
Have the cables ceased to be operated ?

I think they are spasmodically worked, but they are used very little. This is the line which connects Belle Isle with Quebec, and it is the line upon which the shipping of the St. Lawrencei depends to communicate with Quebec.
They have what my hon. friend from Colchester (Mr. Gour-ley) calls lucid intervals ?

Eucid intervals.
Chicoutimi-St. Charles telegraph line, branch from Ste. Anne to Lac Clair, $1,800.
It is proposed to construct a branch line fifteen miles in length from Ste. Anne to Lac Clair, at a cost of .$1,800.

Before we conclude with this vote of $40,000 for Dominion telegraph lines, I would like to ask what is being done to relieve the people of Prince Edward Island from the telegraph monopoly under which they suffer ?

As my hon. friend, who is an old parliamentarian, and a resident of Prince Edward Island, knows this matter has been under discussion for many years. It was brought to my attention this session, and I have taken it up in earliest. As the hon. Minister of Justice has just stated to the committee, legal qirestions have been raised, and they have been referred to the Justice Department for their opinion. The company have made a statement of their claims to the Department of Justice, and we will have their advice in regard to the matter. We are proceeding upon the assumption that there is no monopoly. I think my hon. friend (Mr. Haclcett) will see that the discussion might more properly take place when the item for the subsidy is under consideration. It will be more proper and the information would be far more satisfactory, as I am not prepared at the present time, not having any item in reference to Prince Edward Island before me, to give the information that I would like to give to the hon. gentleman and to the committee. If my hon. friend would be kind enough to bring this question up when the question of the subsidy is under discussion, I am sure that he will find that the government will be ready to discuss it and to give him all the information.

That is quite correct, but I consider the remarks made by the hon. Minister of Justice as being very unsatisfactory in regard to Prince Edward Island. I would like to ask him as the legal adviser of the Crown If he thinks Prince Edward Island is subject to this monopoly ?

This is a question that arose previous to confederation, and results from legislation that was enacted at that time. I understand that parliament has in recent years proceeded on the assumption that there is no monopoly, and as a result of legislation that was introduced this session, the company have thought it proper to make certain representations to the government which representations amount to the statement that they enjoy a monopoly under the legislation that they have. These statements have been referred to the Department of Justice, but I only received the memorandum from the company yesterday. My hon. friend will see that to give a matter of that importance the attention which it requires so as to enable me to give an opinion to the House that would be of any value would take much more time than it is possible at the present stage of the session for me to give to it. I have no desire whatever to make light of the pretensions of Prince Edward Island. If there is a monopoly it seems to me that it would be proper for the government to interfere and to endeavour in some way to get rid of it, but the hon. gentleman cannot expect me to make a statement as to the legal position of the ease or as to the policy of the government without that knowledge which would enable me to make a statement that would be of any value.

I am very thankful for this explanation of the hon. Minister of Justice. I know that he is sincere and honest, and I trust that when he looks at the papers which he says only came into his hands yesterday, that he will give the benefit of any doubt that may arise to the province of Prince Edward Island.
Petite RiviSre-St. Agnes telegraph line, $2,500.

This Is a vote of $2,500 to provide, accords ing to an estimate submitted by the general superintendent of government telegraph lines, for the construction of two lines of telegraph in Charlevoix county, so as to connect St. Agnes, St. Urbain and Petite Riviere.
Are these new lines or are they in substitution for lines already existing ?	.

These are new lines, but extensions of the present lines.
Mr. MORIN* Does the hon. Minister of Public Works know where Petite Riviere is ?

St. Urbain is about midway between Baie St. Paul and St. Agnes. Petite Rivi&re St. Francois is some distance west of Baie St. Paul.
Telephone line to Edmonton Indian agency,
This is to connect Edmonton with the Indian agency, 14 miles distant.
Where is the agency V
It is 14 miles from Edmonton.
What is the name of the place ?

It is tlie Indian reserve at which Mr. Gibbons is the Indian agent.
Telegraph line between Edmonton and Athabasca landing, $15,000.

This is to make provision in accordance with the estimate of the superintendent general of government telegraph lines for the Edmonton-Athabasca line, the distance between the two places being estimated at 100 miles. The total cost of the work for 100 miles is estimated at $150 a mile, making $15,000.
Are the mounted police at Athabasca Landing ?

The mounted police are exercising authority at Athabasca with a number of isolated detachments, and they can only communicate with Edmonton by using the road. The line is principally for the mounted police, but, of course, my hon. friend knows that the country is settling up. There is no railway communication and there is a very considerable number of settlers going In. This has been urged very earnestly by the local authorities at Edmonton, and also by the mounted police. It will be constructed by tender an'd contract.

What leads the minister to decide as to the necessity for such a work as this ? It looks to me that $15,000 is a small sum with which to build 100 miles of telegraph line in such a country. Has the minister the report of an expert ?

My experience is that the superintendent there is a very competent and energetic officer, and this vote is based on his estimate. It is on his report that I ask for the sum, and I have no reason to believe from my past experience of him, and his general ability, but that this will complete the work.
Loop line from a point on the main line near Victoria Alta, to connect with Aedrews, $600.
This is for the construction of four and a half miles of line, the residents agreeing to supply the poles. There is unite a settlement there.

That costs more than $100 a mile.
Extension of telegraph line from Wood Mountain Post to Willow Bunch, $7,600.

This is for thirty-eight miles of land line. There is some difference in the cost in different localities, but that depends on the distance that they have to haul the supplies. This estimate would make it $200 a mile. I may say that our representative from tlie west was here a short time ago. and on looking into the matter I found that the re-Mr. CLARKE.
ceipts have increased fifty per cent last year, so that if they continue at that ratio of increase, the receipts would soon be equal to the expenditure and maintenance.
What rates are charged ?
Tlie rates average from twenty-five cents for ten words to forty-eight cents, according to the distance. They are not unreasonable rates at all.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Are Mr. Charleson and Mr. Rochester up there superintending the construction of telegraph lines ?

They are not. They have not been in this part of the country at all. This work is done under the supervision of the department, and the officer in charge is Mr. McDonald. Mr. Rochester is still in the Yukon, and is in Vancouver at the present time, and Mr. Charleson has just returned to Ottawa.
The cost of one of these lines is $100 a mile; of the other $150 a mile, and of this last one $206 a mile.
In one case the poles are being supplied by the settlers.
That is where the cost is $150 a mile, and it makes the discrepancy all the greater.

I should point out that one of these is a loop line, a double line. The very fact that the officer in charge does vary his estimate according to the locality, shows that he knows what he is doing. It will be easily understood that where you have to cart poles a distance of a couple hundred miles, it might easily double the cost.
Is this work let by contract ?
It is let by contract as a rule.
Have you any means of checking whether or not you are charged too much ?

Oh yes; there are men accustomed to do that sort of work and I think we get a very low price. My difficulty is that the contractors are complaining that they have lost money in some cases. On the short lines, where the settlers find the poles, our own men string the wires.
Was the Canadian Pacific Railway Company asked for an offer to extend this line from their own line at Moosejaw ?
In these sparsely settled districts "on the

north shore of the St. Lawrence, and up in the west, we cannot get the companies to extend their lines. Where settlement is coming in a telegraph line is found to be a great convenience, as the settlers are a long way from the railway and other conveniences.

There is no doubt that telegraphic communication should be established, but I question whether the receipts are sufficient to indemnify the government for the expenditure. If the receipts are as considerable as my hon. friend says, it is probable that the Canadian Pacific Railway Telegraph Company would have been prepared to undertake to build this line without any expenditure whatever to the country. My hon. friend is aware that the telegraph line to the Yukon cost us a considerable sum. Indeed, there were rival companies competing for the privilege of building that line, and offering the most favourable conditions to the government, including the control of rates and free transmission to the government itself. Under these circumstances, it was a very questionable step.

My hon. friend will see that this is not analogous to that. My hon. friend is perfectly right in saying that it would pay the 'company to extend a line here, but they will not do so. As I said before, owing to the increase of settlement in the country, the time appears to be arriving when the expenses will commence to be met by receipts.
Kamloops-Nicola telephone line, re-setting of poles and general repairs, $1,000.
This vote is called for by the general superintendent of telegraphs to provide for the resetting of poles and general repairs on this line, which is sixty-seven miles long.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: Is Mr. Charleson superintending this line ?
No, he has just returned to Ottawa from the Yukon.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: He is still in the employ of the government ?

Yes.
Vancouver Island-Salt Spring Island telephone line-extension, $900.

This vote is to provide for estimates submitted by the general superintendent of telegraph lines to construct this line 'eight miles further on Salt Spring Island. He reports that if the line is exftnded as proposed, it will be so much utilized ns to prove self-sustaining.

I would like to know from the hon. minister if there is any idea on the government side of the House that
the Anglo-American Telegraph Company hold a monopoly of the telegraphic communication between Prince Edward Island and the mainland ?

My hon. friend the Minister of Justice has stated that the government assume that the company have no monopoly, and have been acting accordingly during the present session of parliament, that the company have filed a statement with the government claiming under the contract that they have a monopoly, and that the matter is now under the consideration of the Department of Justice.

Does the government propose to take any action to redress the grievances of the people of Prince Edward Island to which we have been calling attention several times during this session, and for years past ?

I made a statement in reference to this matter a few minutes ago, and perhaps it would be as well for my hon. friend to bring it up again in a day or two, when there will be an opportunity ; and in the interval I will look into the papers as far as possible, and if I can make a statement of any value to the House, I shall be glad to do so. I have not yet been able to look into the papers.
I might refer the hon. Minister of Justice to a speech delivered by the Hon. Senator Ferguson in the Senate a few days ago, in which he reviewed the situation from the beginning.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I would draw the attention of the hon. member to the fact that the discussion on this question is quite irrelevant to this item. He cannot go into a discussion of the monopoly in Prince Edward Island under an item in reference to Vancouver Island.

I understood that w*e could discuss any system of government telegraphs under the question of government telegraphs, which is now before the House. I do not wish to go into a lengthy discussion of this Prince Edward Island telegraphic communication, as the Minister of Justice says he will look into the matter, and we shall have an opportunity to discuss it later on. But I wish to refer to the fact that Senator Ferguson took this matter ut>
in the Senate a few days ago and dealt with it from the beginning, throwing a good deal of light on the contract and on the decision given in regard to the monopoly, on an appeal from a Bill which was passed in this House regulating marine telegraphs in 1874, when the English authorities discountenanced any idea of a monopoly between the island and the mainland. If the Minister of Justice will bring the matter up at a later date during this session, and will let us know what the intention of the govern-

ment is in regard to it, we will let it drop for tlie present.
Arbitrations and awards, including payments authorized, notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act, $5,000.

This is to enable the department to pay the expenses of investigations and necessary arbitrations in connection with claims. We find that we can often settle these claims by having some of our own officials or outside experts to arbitrate between the parties, and in that way save a great deal of money.
What is the reason of this reference to the Civil Service Act ?
Some of the officials of the government might be more competent to undertake this work than outsiders, and out of this money we will pay their expenses when they are sent away from headquarters.
Extra pay besides their salaries ?
Hardly extra pay. If these disputes can be settled by our own officials it will be very much cheaper to use them than to engage outsiders.
Are there any cases pending at the present time ?

I am sorry to say there are some claims. These are often small matters, but they give a good deal of trouble. There are continually disputes between the architect, the engineers in charge and the contractors. I am sure that by having an item like this, we shall save a good deal to the country.
Does this cover the commissions to investigate ?
A small commission will be paid out of this.
What is the nature of the dispute ?

Questions of constructions of contracts and specifications. My hon. friend will know from experience that difficulties are continually arising, and it saves a great deal of trouble and expense to have these matters amicably settled.

If this is not to be a gratuity to the civil service but merely to cover expenses, when they are employed on investigations, wliy do you insert the words ' notwithstanding anything to the contrary in the Civil Service Act.'

Very often the disputes are left to the decision of a man of experience in another department, and a small allowance would not Mr. LEFURGEY.
be out of the way for the trouble and expense.
Will this amount of $5,000 be paid to nobody else but civil servants ?

Occasionally we may go outside the service. The contractor might think that a government employee was biassed, but we find it less expensive to employ a civil servant, when the contractor will consent.
For my part, although this is a vague vote, I would not object to having it employed in remunerating the civil service if necessary.

We have the same vote every year in the Railway Department, and we find that it has worked to advantage.
Chief engineer's office-salaries of engineers, draughtsmen, and . clerks, notwithstanding anything in the Civil Service Act, $14,000.

This is an additional amount required for 1903-4. The reason the words ' notwithstanding anything to the contrary of the Civil Service Act ' are inserted is because a great many of these civil servants are technical officers and do not come under the Civil Service Act.
If they do not, why insert these words ?

Because under the Civil Service Act we could not pay over $400 a year, and these technical officers have salaries averaging from $1,000 to $3,000 a year. Even the chief engineer of the department comes under this vote.
I thought the hon. minister informed the committee that these were officers who did not come under the Civil Service Act.

They do come under the Act unless the vot% is taken with this provision. The Auditor General would not pay them unless they had the vote taken in this way. The chief engineer could not draw his salary otherwise.
Surveys of headwaters of the Ottawa river and tributaries with a view of devising a scheme for the regulation of the water levels of the upper reaches of these streams so as to afford increased facilities for navigation purposes, the descent of timber, &c., $20,000.
On whose recommendation is this expenditure being made ?

A large deputation of the parties interested waited upon the Premier and the government some time ago and made representations with regard to this matter. In this connection I may say that the Dominion

received very considerable revenue which would be increased if the works would be carried out as urged by this deputation. A survey was promised with the view of devising the scheme for the regulation of the water level on the upper reaches of the stream.
What is the estimated cost of the work ?

It is estimated by the chief engineer of the department that this is the lowest amount for which the work can be done. It is a very important question, and the information to be gained is stich information as the public should have.
What is it estimated that the total cost will be ?
It is estimated that the cost will be covered by this vote.
Is this the first appropriation of this kind ?
So far as my information goes, this is the first appropriation for this purpose.
What is the need for It?

The country receives a very considerable revenue from these water-ways, and representations have been made to the government by the parties interested that very great improvements should be made. Qualified engineers will be sent out to see whether or not this is a practical proposition.
What counties is this in ?
Principally, I think, in Wright, Pontiac and Renfrew.

It seems to me I heard that at the time the representatives of the lumbermen waited on the government they submitted a scheme which would render surveys unnecessary and merely call for the execution of certain works.

The chief engineer informs me that they did not submit any detailed scheme. In a general way they pointed out the advantages to be derived if a scheme could be devised to carry out the idea they proposed. The chief engineer reported to me that it was necessary to make the surveys, and this estimate is to defray the cost.
This seems a very large amount. Can the work not be done for less ?

There is a good deal of territory to go over, and much time will be spent by a considerable staff of engineers. The chief engineer
Informs me that it will require at least four parties to do the work in one season, so my hon. friend (Mr. Hackett) will see that this is not a large estimate. I have no personal knowledge of the matter, but this is done on the recommendations of the officials of the department.
When did the deputations wait on the government ?
The last deputation was on the 30th of May.
Has the hon. minister any estimate of the probable cost of the undertaking Contemplated ?

No. The object of the survey is to obtain the levels, because it would be a great mistake to go into any of these works until we have a fair knowledge whether it is practically as represented, and what advantage we shall derive, and what the cost is likely to be.
Will these surveys be conducted by officers of the department ?

That was my intention, to send out the best officers we have in the department at the head of these parties. This I would do for two reasons. First, because they have some knowledge of the matter ; and, secondly, because we should have their services at a less cost than that of others.
May we expect the report of the surveyors at the next session ?
No, it will be a year from next session probably before we have the report.
Have the government no knowledge on this subject now ?
No information. My hon. friend (Mr. Osier) knows that the districts to be surveyed are a long way from headquarters and in the unsettled parts of the country.
How does the matter come up now ?
There is a great deal more use for the power than there was.
This is to devise ' a scheme for the regulation of the water levels, so as to afford increased facilities for navigation purposes, the descent of timber, &c.'

My hon. friend is aware that at certain seasons, when the water is low, the city of Ottawa, for instance, is very much interested in the question of this water-power. It is important to see that we have water enough for navigation and still use water to provide power.
Wliat stretch of country is it proposed to cover ?
I would not like to say off-hand, but, speaking under correction, about 175 or 200 miles.
Have any of these water privileges been disposed of by the government within the last twelve months ?
So far as I am aware, they were all disposed of years ago.
I speak of the privileges far up on the river. Have any of these been disposed of ?	.
Not to my knowledge.

I would like to get a little more light on the subject. Is it to aid the lumbermen that these expenditures are made ? Is it to develop and make more permanent the water-powers, the privilege of which has been secured by private parties ?
That is one of the
Is it not an extraordinary thing for the House to be asked to vote $20,000 to improve these privileges that do not belong to the Crown ?
They belong to the Crown, but have been leased to these parties.
Will the lessees pay an increased indemnity to the Crown because of the work contemplated ?
If we went on with the work, certainly. If we did not receive an increased revenue, we would not go on with the work.

I understand the minister to say that this vote is asked for the purpose of making surveys and obtaining the levels of the river with a view to constructing works to give a more equable supply of water in the Ottawa river ?
Yes, for regulating the water.
If this is done primarily to advantage private persons, I think they ought to contribute some of the cost.

For general navigation also. It is a proper work for the government to undertake when they are to receive a revenue from it. The discussion now going on would be in place if it was proposed to go on with any of these works.
Is this .$20,000 to be expended entirely on surveys ?
Yes.
I still think that if these powers have been leased, the expense of the survey ought to be paid partly by those who are to benefit by the construction of the work.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I understood the minister to say a moment ago that we derived large revenues from these works. I have looked carefully into the public accounts, and fail to find one of these works that produces any revenue. They appear to be like the canals, it costs two or three dollars to collect one dollar of revenue that you get from any of these timber slides and booms. I would like the minister to point out a few of these works that are producing a revenue over and above expenditure.
I think we receive at the present time between $70,000 and $80,000 per annum from the works to be affected by these improvements.

I see by the Auditor General's Report, page W-51, that a sum of $700 has been paid to Henry A. F. MacLeod, civil engineer, for completing unfinished plans and profiles of the Ottawa river survey, made in the autumn of 1900 and the winter of 1901. That would lead us to believe that there had been a survey going on of the Ottawa river.
That has nothing at all to do with the object of this vote. That was in connection with the Georgian Bay canal.

I see also that we voted in main estimates, under the head of miscellaneous surveys and inspections, $50,000. Now, I understood at the time that that was to cover all surveys of any kind that would be made by the Department of Public Works. Now, that $50,000 is a very large amount. I understand that the department has a regular staff that does this work, and therefore I suppose that the minister would simply take a staff away from one work to another; or is it the intention to employ an outside staff independently of those that have been employed in the department for some time ?

That survey as was explained at the time, was part of the ordinary work of the department. We could not apply any part of that money for special work of this kind. We would utilize the staff we have now in the department so far as we could. But to undertake a work of this kind requires some extra assistance.

If the hon. minister sent an engineer and a few men to make a survey of any work under his department, not only in the Ottawa river but in any other part of the country, I see no reason why they should not be paid out of that $50,000.
We have work in the department that requires all that vote, we could not undertake this work under that item.

If he is going to employ an additional staff of engineers to do this work over and above the regular staff, I can quite understand that he requires a certain amount. But it did seem to me that $20,000 was a large amount for surveys.

I cannot offer any opinion as to that. 1 have asked for this amount on the careful report of the engineer, endorsed by Mr. Gobeil, the chief of the department. There is no object in asking for a vote greater than is required.
