Have there been any petitions presented asking for this to be done ?

Yes, I have stated several times that a deputation waited upon the government on the 30th .of May last, composed of certain of the largest business men in this district, men interested in the Ottawa Valley. I cannot give their names at present, but they are well known in this district. They made such representations about the importance of this work that the Premier asked me to make provision for this survey.
Were these men on the deputation lumbermen ?

Principally lumbermen, including Mr. Booth, Mr. Edwards, and others whose names I do not remember. I was present only for a few moments myself, on account of another meeting I had to attend. But it was certainly a very large and influential deputation and after hearing that deputation the right hon. Prime Minister asked me to make provision for having this work carried out.
Would this scheme interfere with the Georgian bay canal ?
It would not interfere, but it would afford very valuable information if it was thought necessary to undertake that scheme.

I do not think it would hurt the Georgian bay canal scheme, but could this project of raising the levels of the upper. Ottawa be carried out as well as the Georgian bay canal scheme ? Could you interfere with the levels of the Ottawa river if the Georgian bay canal were constructed ?

It could not possibly injuriously affect it. My hon. friend has asked if this scheme can be carried out if the Georgian bay canal should prove a practicable proposition. The chief engineer says, yes, that it will help it.
How far up do you intend to survey the tributaries of the river so as to form basins to regulate the*level of the water ?	*
Is there such a work as this constructed in any part of Canada or in any part of the United States ?

There is a work on the Trent river, and there are works in the province of Quebec which they have found to be of great advantage in connection with some of the streams there. They are under the jurisdiction of the provincial government.

Would it not interfere with some of the lumbermen above the Ottawa river where they have slides and booms made to bring their logs down, by raising the water, and thus causing it to back up so that they could not get a sufficient flow of water 1

My object in getting this information is to know whether it would interfere with any one's rights. The question will have to' be considered as to how it will affect any rights that may exist. It would not do to make improvements if they were going to injuriously affect interests upon other parts of the river.
What success has followed the investment of capital in similar works on the Trent river ? Have the parties been satisfied with the amount of money that has been received from the investment ?

These works were erected on the Trent river some years ago and they are under another department. I was asked the question as to whether there were any similar works in existence, and I just recollected these on the Trent river.

I am a great believer in having an investigation made before money is expended, and I am very glad to learn that in one small case at all events the government are of that opinion. It is a wise and proper thing to have a most thorough investigation made in connection with the waters of the upper Ottawa, but the hon. minister made the statement just now that a deputation composed largely of lumbermen had waited upon the government and that it was at the instigation practically of these gentlemen that this item had been put in the estimates.
I said that I understood it was as a result of the representations they had made.
Yes. The Minister of Public Works also said that he thought that the government derived a revenue of $70,000 a year from the lease of these water-powers. I would like very much indeed to
I gave the information furnished by the deputy minister.
I think it would be very interesting if we had the details of that. Perhaps the hon. minister could not give them now.
No, but I would be very pleased to ask that a statement be made out, and I will bring it down probably in a couple of days.

If the government make this investigation it would be very useful to the lumbermen and all those who are interested in the trade of the Ottawa river, although I hope the government are not going to give these lumbermen or any one else the use of the valuable privileges that may be ascertained to exist there as a result of this survey, without putting them up to public competition ; because, if they do, I think it will show that this is merely a scheme to enable some individual lumbermen to pay the expense of enabling them to acquire cheaply the valuable water-powers of the Ottawa river. The government should let these and other water-powers by tender, and only for a short time. These water-powers are going to be enormously valuable. I hope the government will not consider for a moment the alienating of any of the water-powers that exist on the upper Ottawa.
Would the hou. minister tell us where those works on the Trent river are ?

At the head-waters of the Trent. The matter came before me in connection with some claim of the Gilmour firm some time ago. In regard to what my hon. friend from West Toronto (Mr. Osier) has said I quite agree with the position he has taken. If as a result of this survey, it is found that a great improvement can be made, I think every consideration should be given to the question as to how these water-powers should be disposed of. .1 agree with the view of my hon. friend that the country is entitled to see that it gets the greatest possible revenue that is to be had from these water-powers in open competition.
Mr. REID (Grenville. I think it is necessary to have a survey of the river, and I am surprised to learn that an investigation of this kind has not been undertaken before now. I would like to ask the hon. minister if it is really a fact that we have not a chart of the Ottawa river for navigation purposes up to the head of the river. Suppose I went into the department to get a chart

I in order that a steamer might be run to the head waters of the Ottawa, would the department have to admit that there never had been a survey made, and that they could give no information whatever as to the depth of the water on the upper Ottawa ?

We have some information as to the stream itself, as far as navigation is concerned, but no regular chart. I am told by the deputy and by the chief engineer, who have been for many years in the department, that we have no information of that kind.
What does the minister mean by the ' head waters of the Ottawa river.'
I understood by looking at the maps that it might be somewhere around Mattawa. I do not know how much further north it goes.

The minister displays a good deal of ignorance about the head waters of the Ottawa river. Twenty years ago I travelled twenty miles beyond that, and did not reach the head waters. What scheme lias the government in mind with regard to this matter 7
I cannot hear the hon. gentleman.
Then there is the peculiarity that I cannot hear the Minister of Public Works and he cannot hear me. What part of the upper Ottawa does he intend improving 7
My hon. friend from Nipissing (Mr. Mc-Cool), says that we can go 500 miles before we get to the head waters of the Ottawa.
It is above Slattawa then 7

Yes, a long way. I was speaking as the crow flies, but it is a very winding river, and anyhow I do not think that so far as this vote is concerned, that distance makes much difference. Requests have been made to the department for extensive improvements on the Ottawa river, and its tributaries for the purpose of navigation, and to maintain the water-power. I have asked for this vote on the advice altogether of the technical officers of the department. I submit that it would not be a business-like proceeding to ask parliament for any considerable amount of expenditure without having surveys made, and if possible the estimated cost.
Why do you not appiy that principle to the Grand Trunk Pacific 7
One at a time ; I am responsible for this.

These surveys are to benefit the lumbermen, and these improvements would no doubt increase the value of the timber limits. As the timber belongs to the provinces, I contend that an expenditure which would increase the value of the limits should be made by the provinces. It is said that surveys for a railroad through a new country cost about five per cent of the value of work to be undertaken, which would make this expenditure $400,000. Of course it will take a much greater sum than that to carry out the improvements the minister has in view, because these are days of very large enterprises, which have to be rushed through, as we have been given to understand that even time does not wait, and, that we cannot say to-morrow, and to-morrow, and to-morrow. It should be remembered that the government have appointed a transportation commission, and would it not be well that that commission might inquire into all these things ? The Ottawa river runs some 500 or 000 miles beyond Ottawa, and I presume that the government are not going to get to its head waters with this survey. There is a vote lower down for a ' transportation commission ' which, I take it for granted, is not the transportation commission which the government has announced with such a flourish of trumpets. I contend that before you go into this expenditure, this matter should be brought before the commission and it should be made one of these things that the government would deign to refer to it, so that in years hence when we come to improve the navigation of the Ottawa river we may have this information in the report of the commission. If the transportation commission is to have nothing to do with our large railways, and with expenditures on our harbours, surely something might be referred to it. I contend that this is one of the things which it would be well to leave in the hands of this transportation commission. I can assure the hon. minister that it will relieve him wonderfully. Instead of having to answer questions for an hour or an hour and a half, lie can with one sweep of his hand say : There is the report of the transportation commission ; read it. It will be of great benefit to the government this session, and to the government that will follow next session. I hope wTe shall be able to make good use of this transportation commission, which the government at present seem to be ignoring.

My hon. friend has given another strong argument, which I had not thought of, in favour of gathering this information. It was intended to be in connection with the navigation of the river, but it is possible, as my hon. friend says, that in the near future the information may be of great service to the country in connection with a greater scheme of navigation.
41 SI

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I have no doubt that this item was put in the estimates for the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. MeCool) and the deputation he may have come with. No doubt he is acquainted with the district, and can give us some information as to the probable result of the gurvey, and as to whether navigation on these waters can be benefited.

I may say that I was not present with the deputation which the minister speaks of, but I know the object of the vote, it is not to build dams alone, but is for a general survey of the river. There is a large body of water at Lake Temiscaming, and it would be difficult to erect a dam there. Then there are Quinze and Expanse lakes, where a very short dam would control the water and give a basin of 100 square miles. At Lake Victoria there are about 200 square miles of water, and the outlet is very narrow. There are good high banks in both cases, so that a very small expenditure would control the water. The dam would hold the water during the spring freshets, and by means of gates its flow could be regulated, so that during the dry summer season there would be a good flow. The lumber industry would be benefited by having a fair flow of water at all seasons for driving purposes. Navigation would also be benefited and a great deal of the expense that has to be borne at present for dredging would be done away with. There is a dredge on Lake Temiscaming at the present time which would not have been necessary if this scheme had been carried out. There is sufficient water at medium height ; but in spring it is higher than is required, while during the dry summer season the water recedes so that it is impossible to get near the shore. I think this is a very wise and necessary expenditure. A survey of the Ottawa river from here to Mattawa was made about fifty years ago by Mr. Walter Shanley. That was the only survey, and it was very carefully made. I read the report of it in the library a short time ago. From Mattawa west there has not been a survey made at all. On Lake Temiscaming, which is really an, expansion of the Ottawa river, there are eight or ten boats, which carry a very large quantity of freight.

I do not propose to offer an adverse criticism to this appropriation ; but where large public works are contemplated, it is necessary that the fullest information should be given by the government. This grant for surveys evidently contemplates a possible outlay at no distant date of a very large amount of money for improvements on the Otttawa river, and I would like to know what is the net revenue derived from the various franchises that would be benefited by these public works ?

At the present time I am informed the rev-

enue is between $70,000 and $80,000 per annum.

If the records are looked over, they will show that though there has been a considerable amount of money spent on building slides and dams on the Ottawa river and its tributaries* the expenditure has been repaid to the government twenty times over. They have been one of the greatest sources of revenue the government have had in the past, considering the amount of money expended.
What would be the probable increase in the revenue from the proposed expenditure ?
It is decreasing.

I cannot give any opinion as to the probable increase. The expenditure on these improvements, I presume, would be very large. Before making that expenditure it was thought advisable to have a careful examination and report made by qualified engineers.

We have had a very rosy assurance from the hon. member for Nipis-sing (Mr. McCool) that this is not only a good thing for the country, but a profitable investment. If I understood him correctly, the expenditure has paid its way over and over again. I have not taken the trouble to go over the Auditor General's Report for past years, but I presume that last year would be a fair sample.
No, last year would not be. I said the revenue had been falling off.

In the first place, we had the statement of the Minister of Public Works that the revenue last year was some $70,000 or $80,000. I find on page V-394 that the revenue for the Ottawa district was $37,923.23; for the St. Maurice district, $13,565.48 ; and for the Newcastle district, $5,847.22, or, instead of being $70,000 or $80,000, it was $57,335. The expenditure on these services last year was : For the St. Maurice district, including staff and repairs, $51,727 ; for the Ottawa district, $42,182 ; and for the whole service, $201,958. It would seem that hon. gentlemen have been groping in the dark in regard to this question.

I did not include the St. Maurice river at all. It did not enter into my calculation. I know nothing about the St. Maurice and am speaking about the Ottawa river, and if you take the accounts that are to be found in the department for the last twenty-five years, you will find that my sstatement is absolutely correct.
If I take the Ottawa river, the hon. gentleman is in the same difficulty, because the expenditure largely exceeded the receipts last year in the Ottawa district alone.
One year would not be a fair test because they may have had large extra expenditure in rebuilding improvements, which I know to have been the case.

I am afraid my hon. friend has been speculating in that way very generally. I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Public Works to state just how this vote came to be in the estimates. Is there any portion of this work which should be properly done by private enterprise ?

On the 30th of May last a very large and influential deputation waited upon the First Minister and represented that the public was very much interested in having some work done there. We felt in the department that we had not the necessary information to ask the House to grant a vote, and for that reason we have suggested that a survey be made and an examination by qualified engineers into the practicability of carrying on the work, and also as to its cost before spending a dollar in connection with it.

The hon. gentleman seems to be more cautious in small matters than in large. We have had an expenditure involving some hundreds of millions of dollars undertaken, and the government did not think that the same precaution should be used in both cases. I would ask if the deputation made any financial representation regarding the cost of the work '!

I think that I might divide the representations made by those people under three headings. First, the regulation of navigation of the river; second, regulating the water so as to bring down the logs; third, regulating the water-powers which are of such great value to this district, supplying, as they do, this House and city with light and water.
Has there been any undertaking by those persons to pay higher rental and to recoup the treasury for its outlay ?

No, the representations made were solely in the public interest. It will be for us, having charge of the work, to say upon what terms any advantages should be given to parties outside of the general public.
The demand of the deputation was not for surveys but for the expenditure of a large sum and it was the government which suggested that the survey should be first made.
Yes.
What amount was it contemplated that the work would cost ?
No one was in a position to make an estimate, but we all know that at that distance the cost would be very considerable.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I understand from the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. McCool) that only a couple of dams are required, one at the foot of a lake 200 miles long, and another at the foot of another lake one hundred miles long. It would certainly not cost much to put in a couple of dams, but does not the hon. member know that if the water is raised at these outlets, great damage will be done to surrounding land ?

Not at this point, because there are no settlements there except a few lumber camps. I repeat that the expenditure will not be very much, though of course the cost of putting in a dam and bringing out supplies will be heavier than in the case of a dam built in this neighbourhood. But the expenditure would not be very large because the mouths at the outlet of those expansions are not very wide or very deep. Then, another point is the Kippewa lake. That, I presume, is another hundred miles. As I am on my feet, I might mention that I have a memorandum showing that the receipts of the Ottawa slides and booms for last year increased by $8,100 over the previous year. I was surprised to learn this as I thought the receipts were falling off year by year. Still another point is that this survey should include work with a view to using the power of the different falls along the Ottawa up to its head. Take, for instance, the Chats, Portage du Fort, Rocher Fendu. Des Joachim. Roches Capitaine, and othgr rapids and falls. I suppose that between here and Lake Temiskamingue, it would be possible to develop 300,000 or 400,000 horse-power.

I was inclined to look favourably on this vote, but since the explanation given by the hon. member for Nipissing, it occurs to me that it is utterly misapplied money. From what I saw when I was in the district of Nipissing a year ago, I think it would be far more useful to spend money in improving the roads for the settlers of that district than in such a work as this. There are other improvements far more needed in Nipissing, such as wharfs, railway facilities and others. If I understood my hon. friend (Mr. McCool) correctly, it is to dam the Ottawa river in such a way as to keep the level of the river higher, this being particularly for the advantage of the lumbermen. The wants of that district are not confined to the lumbermen, and I venture to say that far more useful employment could be found for this money, and the benefits of its expenditure much more generally extended among the inhabitants of the district. My hon. friend knows that the lumbermen are not a penurious class of people. They want improvements so as to
ensure the better floating of their logs, and so they came to the government. If these gentlemen wish to make larger profits out of their business by having a more uniform water level, and wish to saddle the government with the construction of the dams, why should not they bear a certain share of the expenditure by having these surveys made themselves and a reasonable plan placed before the government of the improvements they require ? There is another point, and one to which I would ask my hon. friend's particular attention. If the object is merely to dam certain indicated portions of the Ottawa river, surely it does not require $20,000 for that ? If the minister will inquire in the city of Montreal or, no doubt, in the city of Toronto, he will find competent engineers who will make a report as to the work necessary for damming the river and the cost of that work for far less than $20,000. The survey is not going to be made this winter, and there will be plenty of time if the money is voted next session. I understand that we are going to have a session in the early part of the winter to repair some of the mistakes of hon gentlemen opposite. Then we can vote the money with a better knowledge of what we are doing. But I say that for one-quarter of this sum the minister will find engineers to carry out the surveys for this work as the hon. member for Nipissing has explained it. Under the circumstances, it seems to me that this is not only an expenditure for dams, but a damnable expenditure.

The hon. member for Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) seems to be under the impression that I have some special interest in this vote. I tell him frankly that I did not know even that it was in the estimates until this evening. And, as to benefiting Nipissing particularly, that is not the case. Not one of the dams referred to wouid be built in Nipissing, but most of the work would be done in the hon. gentleman's own province, for nearly all the dams I hav e spoken of are in the province of Quebec. But this is a national work. The hon. gentleman need not imagine that I am advocating it because it is only going to benefit Nipissing or any friends of mine.

If the work is to be done in the province of Quebec, the river being between Quebec and Ontario, it must extend into Ontario also. But if the work is to be confined to the province of Quebec, I can tell my hon. friend the Minister of Public Works that we have engineers in the city of Montreal, qualified under the laws of the province of Quebec, who will be able to make a .full and complete report on this subject for less than $5,000. So, what is the use of spending $20,000 ?

Had the hon. gentleman (Mr. Monk) been

present lie would have heard me explain that this estimate was based on the report of the engineers of the department. It is a question for the Committee to decide whether to take the advice of my hon. friend, who knows practically nothing of the work to be done, the miles to be covered, or the time likely to be occupied, or that of the experienced officers of my department. The hon. gentleman may be right, but for my part, I would rather act on the report of the engineers of the Public Works Department.
Is this money expended with a view to ultimately adopting the Ottawa and Georgian bay canal scheme ?

The information gained might be used in connection with that scheme, as suggested by the hon. member for Centre Toronto (Mr. Brock). But no such idea was in( view at the time of preparing this estimate.

The hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Murray) has on several occasions presented the claims of the Ottawa and Georgian bay canal in a way that enlisted my sympathies to a certain extent. And I have often wondered why the people in Ontario did not insist on opening up the Ottawa river with a view to determining its value in connection with the transportation routes of Canada. If this is a mere local expenditure made on .behalf of the lumber interests in Ontario, I should be opposed to it. But if it is intended to bring information to this House to enable us to know whether the Georgian bay canal is feasible in the interests of the' whole of Canada, the expenditure might be justified. The minister has said it will be useful in this connection only In an indirect way. In that case the expenditure ought not to be made, for it could not be made intelligently with a view to getting that information, unless the engineers were so instructed. To go up the Ottawa and build certain dams which will yield only a certain benefit to the lumber interest, is a thing, I think, we should not be called upon to do. But if, in the larger interests of Canada, it would help to solve the transportation problem, I would support the vote. I have on many occasions, in listening to the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Murray), while speaking of the Georgian bay canal, been struck with the importance of the Ottawa river as a means of communication. I think it should play a very important part in the transportation route .from the Georgian bay to the seapoi'ts, and if the money were voted for that purpose, and engineers were instructed to develop that idea and give us the latest information, I yyould feel like incurring the vote. But if. on the other hand, it is merely in favour of a local interest, I think we ought not to make the expenditure.
Certainly very valuable information will be given in connection with that project.

When I read this item I supposed it was to make a complete survey of the Ottawa river, and I asked the minister if that was the intention, and the minister replied that it was the intention to get a chart of the Ottawa river. Now the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. McCool) stands up and assures us that this is for building dams on the Ottawa river.

The hon. gentleman is ascribing words to me that I never uttered. I did not say that the money was for that purpose, I said that it was the intention of the lumbermen who urge this survey, to ascertain the best means of regulating the spring freshets. I gave my own opinion that that could only be accomplished by dams at the points I named.
Then the member for Nipissing states that this money is to be expended merely for surveys in view of building dams, and not for the Ottawa river at all.
I did not say that at .all.
Did lie not state that this money was to be expended for surveys for dams ?
No, I did not.
The hon. gentleman has just stated that the lumbermen wanted it.
That was their intention.
That this money was to be used for surveys for dams. *

I did not make any such statement. I said this money was appropriated for the purpose, as stated by the Minister of Public Works, of surveying the Ottawa river. The deputation asked for some improvements to regulate the flow of the water, and that is what induced the minister to put this amount in the estimates -to make a complete survey of the Ottawa river.

It looks to me worse and worse. It seems this money is required to get from experts a report as to the best places in the upper stretches of the Ottawa where the river may be dammed, and the only men who are going to get the benefit of this are the lumbermen, they are going to get all the benefit of these expert surveys upon which the government will be asked to make a large expenditure for dams They will get the benefit of all these researches as to the best places where the river may be dammed. These people know exactly where the best water-powers will be, and so the whole of this expenditure is for the lumbermen on the upper Ottawa. Their

trade will be benefited and they will have water-ways of great value. This is not a proper application of public money.

I confess I have had some difficulty in ascertaining the exact purpose for which this money is asked. However, from what 1 learn in this discussion,
I take it for granted that the object of this vote is to devise some system of constructing dams, booms and slides on the river Ottawa and its tributaries, for the purpose of aiding the lumbermen who may go up there and purchase large tracts of timber and float it down the river. Now, if the timber that is to be floated down the Ottawa and its tributaries is still vested in the Crown, still belongs to the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, I think these provinces should construct these improvements for the purpose of making an outlet for the timber which belongs to them. If the property has passed out of the hands of the provinces into the hands of private individuals, who bought it with all these obstructions in the way of navigation, all these difficulties iu the way of getting out their timber, and consequently would buy this timber at a very much reduced price, I do not see that we are called upon at all to improve the river Ottawa and its tributaries for the sole advantage of the men who have purchased the timber at a low price when these facilities were not provided. Now, there is the larger question, to my mind, of provincial rights. We are told that these booms and slides are a profitable investment. If they are, very possibly we may find the provinces complaining that we are trespassing on their rights by constructing these slides and booms and taking away the revenue from them. The provinces are at the present time very jealous of this parliament. We noticed that in the chartering of a railway a short time ago between the cities of Hamilton and Toronto, when they thought their rights were invaded. I think we should be very watchful not to invade the rights of the provinces. In this instance I fear we would be invading their rights, more especially if they are going to obtain a revenue from these improvements, as I understand from the hon. member for Nipissing that they will be a profitable investment. I have some doubts about that. I have looked at the revenue derived from booms and slides that have been constructed. Reference has been made to the St. Maurice river and the amount of money that accrued to the government last year from the large expenditure on that river. But we forget that we are yearly expending large sums of money in order to get that small amount of revenue.
I think that during the present session we have voted 850,000 for improvements and boom works to facilitate the floating and storage of logs on the St. Maurice district. That is about four times as much as the
revenue that was derived last year from that district. I very much fear that the prophesies of the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. McCool) will not be realized if the results are no more gratifying than they have been in the province of Quebec on that river. But, I think, first, that the whole question just depends upon what the object of this expenditure is. Who is to be benefited V If the province of Ontario and the province of Quebec are to be benefited, if their timber is to be increased in value by reason of these improvements, then let Ontario and Quebec construct these works for the purpose of giving increased value to the timber which they own. If we construct these public works at the expenditure of $400,000 or $500,000 it will practically be an additional subsidy given to the provinces, and we will get nothing at all for it. If the property has passed out of the hands of the provinces of Ontario and Quebec, and belongs to private individuals who bought it with all these obstructions in the way of getting it out, and bought it at probably one half of what it would have been worth if these improvements had been made, let these men pay for these improvements, and not ask us to spend the money of the people to benefit private individuals. The hon. Minister of Public Works told us that a large deputation had waited upon the government. I would like to know who composed that deputation. I think if we had the names of the gentlemen who composed that deputation we would find that it comprised the names of many gentlemen who are large holders of timber berths, who purchased these timber berths with these difficulties in the way, and who expect the government to use the money which belongs to the people of the whole Dominion simply to provide improvements to assist them in getting out the timber which they purchased at a low price by reason of those difficulties and that this proposed expenditure is to personally benefit themselves. I do not see the propriety of voting this appropriation at the present time. Although the sum was asked for the purpose of getting information, I think it would be well for the government to wait and see whether it is wise to go any farther. I think we had better consider whether there is any reasonableness in the inquiry which it is proposed to make..

These are Dominion works. These works were transferred to the Dominion at the time of confederation, and they are under its jurisdiction. The Dominion is charged with the maintenance of these works, and collects the revenue from them. My hon. friend (Mr. Henderson) knows very well that Ontario and Quebec do not collect the revenue. Could we undertake any great national work which is not for the benefit of the people of Canada 1 The people of

Ontario and Quebec form a part of this Dominion, and a great national work such as this, I think, would he for the general benefit of Canada. My hon. friend refers to those who may own the timber limits, and he says that they should pay for these improvements. They complain that the fees are too high now. How that may be I do not know, but certainly we do collect a very considerable revenue. My hon. friend im stances the work at the St. Maurice river. Probably if the same care had been taken beforehand to make a survey such as we propose before the work was undertaken, we might have had better work for less money. I am not saying that is so, but it is always better to have information before undertaking a work of this description. I think, having removed the fears of my hon. friend as to who owns these works, and having pointed out the good results that will flow from such an expenditure as we propose to make, he should withdraw his opposition. I could understand the criticism if we were asking for a vote to carry out any of these improvements. Then it would be for each ho'n. member to express his opinion as to whether the improvements were of such a national character as to warrant us in going into them. But we are not doing that to-night. Here is a large question affecting the navigation of the Ottawa river. We hear the hon. member for .Jacques Cartier (Mr. Monk) hour after hour declaiming about the great necessity for improving water navigation, yet, when the slightest effort is made in that direction, it is denounced as a damnable expenditure. It shows that we have hon. gentlemen in this House who have not given the matter very much consideration, and that there is on their part a great deal of talk with very little action. This is a work of great national importance, covering a vast area of territory, and I submit it to the committee, and if the majority think differently from me in regard to the question, they can refuse to pass the vote. This investigation should Ire made at the earliest possible moment, and it will depend on the report of the engineers as to whether in the opinion of parliament any expenditure should be undertaken upon the improvement of the river.
If. I thought the object of the vote was to improve the navigation of the upper Ottawa. I would think more kindly of it.

1 would not come to parliament and ask for a vote without saying that it was for a specific purpose. If the report of the engineers is such that the amount involved is greater than the benefits to be derived, that will be a question for parliament to determine, but certainly it would be a great advantage to have that information, if we Hon. Mr. SUTHERLAND.
are asked to undertake any of that work in the future.

I do not object to that, but I understand that the object of the expenditure even if it is recommended by these engineers, will not be to improve the navigation of the upper Ottawa, or of its tributaries, but to obstruct it by the construction of dams across it, so that instead of the river

My hon. friend is misinformed. The conclusion to be derived from the hon. gentleman's remarks is that we are asking for the money under false pretenses. The statement in the vote itself shows that the improvement of the facilities for navigation is one of the objects in view. The second object, the descent of timber, is incidental thereto, and surely the improvement of the river is in the interest of the country.

I do not insinuate that the hon. gentleman was asking for the money under false pretenses, but as the discussion has gone on, I have learned that it is not so much for the purpose of improving the navigation of the river as practically to obstruct the course of the river in such a way as to destroy it for the purposes of navigation, and that these obstructions will be used in the interests of private individuals. As I said before, in so far as I know, they have acquired large interests in that section of the country which will be vastly improved in value if this expenditure is made.

When application is made to the Department of Public Works, such as it is necessary to make under the law by private individuals or corporations, to make certain improvements on this river, how is the department to know whether they shall be allowed to do so or not if it has no knowledge as to the waters that are to be affected ? This is very important and very necessary information to be acquired by the Dominion of Canada looking to the protection and improvement of this great river.

I am not finding fault with the hon. gentleman taking this step, but what I do doubt is the propriety of doing anything even after he has obtained the information. I have very great doubt as to the propriety of the Dominion government expending public money there at all. In this matter we are invading provincial rights. We are interfering with works that ought to be undertaken by the provinces. If the property has passed out of the hands of the provinces, and has been acquired by private individuals at a time when no improvements were made on the river stretches, and at low prices on account of the difficulties of getting that timber out, then I do not see why we should be called upon to spend large sums of money for the

purpose of making valuable the property that was purchased at a very low price.
On which of the tributaries of the Ottawa are these improvements to be made ?

I am not able to give that information. If my bon. friend is in earnest, he must know that there are a great many tributaries of the Ottawa that have never been surveyed, and I suppose not even named. The improvements will depend upon the report of surveyors. I do not say that any improvements will be made at all, but it is important that we should have information before we expend any money.

I have been asking for a survey from O'Leary station to the west shore of the island which would cost only $1,000, but I have always been refused. While you are spending this $20,000 to survey an unexplored country, you might make that survey in Prince Edward Island and build a wharf there too.
The Ottawa river and its tributaries have had improvements many years ago, and they have served the purpose since. What new conditions have arisen which call for further improvements V

The Ottawa river works were started forty or fifty years ago and we have urgent applications for different works, and we want to get information. The new conditions are the general development of the country. J

I understand that an interprovincial river, as the Ottawa is for some distance, would come within the jurisdiction of this parliament, but has the minister considered how far it devolves upon us to undertake work in any province ?

We would not think of intruding on provincial territory without arranging with the province.
. Mr. CLANCY. I have no doubt that the provinces would not object to an expenditure of money by the Dominion.
Has the hon. gentleman any doubt that the improvement of navigable rivers is under the jurisdiction of this parliament ?
As I understand it, this is not a navigable river, but it is proposed to make it so.
It is navigable now.
What is the draft of the boats that ply on that river ?
Aly information is, that the Ottawa is navigable for 40 miles above Ottawa where we have made improvements. Some of the boats draw from six to eight feet more or less.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The minister should take the advice of the hon. member from Jacques Cartier (Mr. Alonk) and drop this vote for the present session, because he does not purpose sending surveyors out this time of the year.
This is just the time.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hdn. member for Nipissing (Air. McCool) and the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Murray) who are sitting beside the minister, know all about this region, and they can give the minister more information than he will get by sending out a band of surveyors, costing $20,000. Probably these gentlemen accompanied the deputation that wen't to the minister to ask for this vote.
The hon. gentleman should accept the word of the hon. member for Nipissing (All*. McCool) that he did not accompany the deputation, and did mot know the vote was in the estimates until to-night.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: I accept that, but perhaps the member for Pontiac cannot say so much. The hon. member (Mr. AIcCool) knows these waters very well, and lie can give all the information that the minister wants. I would like to hear what the hon. member for Pontiac (Mr. Alurray) has to say.

I may say, that like the hon. member for Nipissing (Mr. AIcCool), I did not accompany any deputation. I am not specially interested in the vote before the House ; but I do know, from my experience as a business man, that the lumber industry is very much interested in these improvements on the upper Ottawa. The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat knows as well as I do that the lumbermen have to go further back to the various tributaries to get out their lumber ; and they get it out late in the season, when the water is low. I do not think there should be any objection to the government expending the appropriation for the purpose named.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext:
The hon. member for Nip-issing (Mr. AIcCool) says that the construction of two dams would do the whole business ; and $20,000 which the government are proposing to spend on surveys, if spent on the work itself, would probably construct those dams.
To provide for expenditure in connection with a transportation commission, $25,000.

There has been so much discussion with regard to this transportation commission that I do not know that there is any further information which I can give upon the subject. Perhaps the commission would have been-organized before this but for the long delay in getting the vote before the House. Every member has a copy of the Order in

Council providing for the commission. I am of opinion that good l-esults will come from the investigation.

The government, having dealt with the transportation problem before getting the information have done away entirely with the need of a commission, and now I do not know what it is required or expected to do.

I understand that this sum of $25,000 is not to pay the salaries of the commissioners, but only to provide for the expenditures in connection with the inquiry. How long is this supposed to last ? Will it pay for a full year or only a portion of a year ? I think we are entitled to some explanation as to when the commissioners are expected to begin their work, and what its scope will be.

I would ask my hon. friend to read the Order in Council, which states better than I could at this time the scope of the inquiry. They will necessarily gather statistics and information at various points in the Dominion from the Atlantic ports to the ports on the lakes, and this vote is to cover the expenditure that they may find necessary for secretaries and for technical and statistical information.

I read the Order in Council of the 19th May last, and I thought that one special object of the appointment of this commission was to deal with the question of transportation from the great west to the east. The question has now been settled by the government themselves, and we do not want a commission to deal with it. They have agreed to spend from $100,000,000 to $150,000,000 in constructing a transcontinental railway to dispose of the whole problem. Consequently if that was the object of appointing the commission, I do not see why $25,000 should be appropriated when the work of the commission has been actually taken out of their hands. I am not going to oppose this vote. I think it is very desirable that the work of this commission should go on. I think a great blunder was committed in not having the commission set to work months ago. If that had been done, possibly many millions of money would have been saved to the people of this country. So let us not hesitate now to appropriate the funds that are necessary to set the commission to work, trusting that good will come from it. I wish not to offer the slightest opposition, but only to express my regret that the government did not take action in this matter many months ago, so that they would have had the recommendations of the commissioners before they had entered on the construction of the transcontinental railway.
I regret that I cannot agree with the hon. member who has just spoken. In view of the action of this par-

liament on the transportation question during the present session and the fact that we have no scheme before us, I cannot see the need of this commission, nor what work there is for it to do. It seems to me that if there ever was a time when we needed a commission, it was before we took the step which we have taken this session ; but that step having been taken, and the transportation problem having been dealt with. I venture to say that there will be very little change from what has been outlined. It is true, we shall be likely to go on and improve our canals, harbours and waterways to some extent ; we shall have to do that of necessity ; but what other great seheme is to be hatched out by this commission I cannot understand, and I think if we go on with it at present, it will be so much money thrown away.

I absolutely oppose, at the present time, the appropriation of one dollar towards this transportation commission. We were all of one mind some months ago as to the desirability of having a transportation commission for the purpose of solving the great transportation question which was then coming up. But after having committed ourselves to an enormous expenditure for the construction of a transcontinental line, after having taken out of the hands of the commission that pressing problem, it would be injudicious to expend this money. It may be quite true that we have many public works in the way of transportation which still require our attention, but there must be a halt called some time in the public expenditure, and in the face of the fact that we have committed ourselves to the construction of a railway which will cost anywhere from one to two hundred million dollars, I do not see why we should go on and spend money on a commission to inquire into the transportation problem which the government has determined to solve without the advice of any commission.
Like the hon. gentleman who has just sat down, I object to this item. Had the railway Bill not passed, I would not have objected to it, but now7 that the whole question is really settled
I am glad the hon. gentleman is1 so easy to satisfy with regard to the transportation question.
The government have settled that question in so far as the construction of a railway is concerned.
I am glad that the hon. gentleman is pleased with our railway policy.
I did not say I was, but that the question has been settled and, so far as this item is concerned, I would move that it be struck out.

I am disposed to support that motion. Had this commission gone on and done the work intended that it should do when it was promised in the speech from the Throne, I would have said that we were doing the right thing in voting the money, but after the government have committed themselves to an expenditure of $125,000,000 to $150,000,000 for the purpose of effectively dealing with the transportation question, I can see no use for this commission. To vote this money would be locking the stable after the horse is stolen. When we add the salaries of the three commissioners and other expenses to this item, we will find that we will have to pay some $75,000 in the near future to keep these men going, and we will be doing that after the only object for which this commission was intended has been settled. We are practically appointing three men for no purpose whatever and at great expense.
What will be the salary to each of these commissioners ?

It is not the intention to pay them any salary, but there will be some allowance paid for their services, depending on the time they will be at work. They will not be salaried men in any sense. The class of men we have appointed are not looking for salaries and never considered that a salary would be paid them.
No doubt somethingl will be paid them for their services.
I suppose some honorarium or something of that kind, but no salary.
There will be a chairman and two commissioners. What is it intended to allow the commissioners as compensation for their services ? Have any arrangements been made with them ?

No, when they meet an arrangement will be made, but I have no idea of considering a salary or that they would ask for a salary -only some allowance to cover their expenses and for the value of the time they give.

I do not think my hon. friend should play on words. We are now voting an expenditure on this commission which will certainly cost $100,000, at the very least, if it sits one year. And, surely, before we vote that money we are entitled to know some details of the proposed expenditure. First and foremost, we are entitled to know what amount should be paid to the commissioners, whether you call it salary, solatium, indemnity for services, compensation for lost time, honorarium, or anything else.
Is it proposed to make a per diem allowance or to pay a Tump s"um 1

As I stated, the commission have no;t met and organized. But some sum will be allowed. I do not expect that it will be paid, except as I have stated. This is to cover the expenses of the commission, and it is not my intention to incur a large expenditure in connection with it without further consulting parliament.

But the trouble is that we commence the expenditure. If, later on, we object, we shall be confronted with the argument, as we have been over and over again in other matters, that we should have objected before. That being the case, this is the time to endeavour to stop this expenditure. The minister says he does not intend to allow the commissioners any salary. To use a common expression, that is entirely too thin.

My hon. friend (Mr. Sproule) misunderstood. I said that no doubt an allowance should be made in accordance with the services rendered. These men would gather certain information and prepare the report.

The country never employs men for such work without paying them handsomely, and no doubt these men will be remunerated on a scale commensurate with that given for similar work. We might as well recognize that at the beginning. But the question with .me is as to the wisdom of paying out this money after having dealt with the transportation question as we have done. It is simply a vote of $25,000 as the beginning of an expenditure that will run up to $100,000. We might as well recognize that that is what we have to face.

I do not think that any member would object to this or a larger sum if it were necessary to have a commission on the transportation question. But we know that the government have been telling us for months that they have solved the whole transportation problem. If so, what is the use of this commission ? It cannot change the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway Bill ; that is settled. I cannot, for the life of me, see what there will be for the commission to do. I believe that this item was put in to hood-wink the people and make them believe the government are carrying out the promise they made early this session to have a commission to solve the transportation question. They think that if they did not put this in they would not be able to defend their action on the Grand Trunk Pacific. Under the circumstances, I have no hesitation in moving that the item be struck out. The motion may not carry, but I believe that it is not fair to vote this item now that the Grand Trunk Pacific legislation has passed this House.

This is a preliminary provision for the transportation commission. Hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House laid great stress on this commission, and said that the Grand Trunk Pacific Bill should have been kept back until the report of the commission was received. Surely, these lion, gentlemen will not say that the only transportation question for the country is the Grand Trunk Pacific question ? Is there not the question of transportation by the St. Lawrence water-way ? Is there not the question of transportation by railways other than the Grand Trunk Pacific ? Is there not the question of the Ottawa and Georgian hay canal, in itself sufficient to occupy the attention of a commission ? For my part, I must say that I never took much stock in the idea of a commission, for it seems to me that the people's representatives should settle questions. But the strong opinion of the House seemed to be that there was a need for a commission. Good men have been selected, and this is a preliminary vote to pay for their services. It is not a large amount, considering the character of the work expected of them.
Amendment (Mr. Reid, Grenville) negatived ; yeas 22, nays 40.
Government of the Yukon Territory-additional amount required for expenses in connection with the administration of the Territory, $15,000 ; amount required for the maintenance and construction of roads and bridges in the Territory, $113,490 ; grant to administration of Yukon Territory for construction and maintenance of public buildings for local purposes and settlement of claims in connection with the construction of roads, $113,500-$241,990.
The latter item of $113,000 is really that for which I am asking a vote here. The money of these three items is paid out through the local council of the Yukon.
Has the money been spent already ?

No. This is an allowance to the Yukon council for constructing the works set forth here. My hon. friend will remember that an arrangement was made by which we voted this money to the council, with the understanding that it would be administered better under the local authorities, since the council has become partly appointed and partly elected, than by the department here.
Pelly river bridge at Lethbridge-reconstruction of-to recoup the government of the North-west Territories, $55,000.
Old Man's river bridge at Maeleod-reconstruction of-to recoup the government of the North-west Territories, $29,000.
Both these bridges were carried away by a freshet in May, 1902. and application was made to the department to rebuild them. An examination was made by the engineer, and

it was thought better to erect more permanent structures than had previously existed. There was some correspondence between the local government and the Dominion as to how the money should be charged, and it was understood that the bridges were to be built by the Dominion.

The item says :	' To
recoup the government of the North-west Territories.'

'The construction of these bridges was urged upon us by the local government as a matter of immediate necessity, and they agreed that we should expend the money out of their vote, to be recouped by this government.

On another item I asked a question this afternoon for a statement of the various items which appear in the different estimates of grants of money for the North-west Territories. We do not know what we are voting in the aggregate, and it is time that we should know that.

The hon. gentleman's request is a very proper one. The deputy made a memorandum, and to-morrow he will have this account made up.
Telegraph lines, British Columbia-working expenses-additional amount required, $2,500.

Are the telegraph lilies self supporting ? Excepting this amount for working expenses, what is the original amount ? What are the telegraph lines costing to-day for maintenance over and above their earnings ?

1 will give that information on the Yukon vote. Mr. Chairman, we have done a little work at any rate, and perhaps we had better rise.
Some resolutions reported.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) moved the adjournment of the House.

Before the House adjourns I would like to state that when the House goes into committee, either to-morrow or on some future day before long, a motion will be made in regard to the expenditure in connection with the taking of the last census. What business does the minister intend to take up to-morrow ?
We will continue in Supply, taking Public Works, and after we finish them, Militia.

There was an arrangement that the Militia estimates should come up to-morrow morning. There was an understanding to that effect with

tlie Minister of Militia and Defence. If the lion. Minister of Finance will be good enough to keep his rank and tile in better control than they were this morning we will get on very much more expeditiously with the estimates than we have done to-day.
I would like the arrangement to be carried out to take up the militia estimates tomorrow.
Arrangement with whom ?
With the Minister of Militia.

I am most willing and anxious to oblige hon. members. I think there was one item allowed to stand affecting the Yukon and there are some small votes for Quebec which I think we can easily dispose of in the morning and then go on with the militia estimates in the afternoon. If hon. gentlemen want any particular item to stand for discussion I shall be perfectly willing, but, unless there is some object I would like to proceed with my estimates because there have been a great many days during this session taken up with the Public Works estimates.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Conservative Party (1867-1942)
speechtext: The hon. Minister of Militia and Defence came over last night and said that he wanted to know if we started his estimates the first thing in the morning it would be possible to get through with them before six o'clock as we are going to adjourn in the evening. My hon. friend from Victoria (Mr. Hughes) said that he had a statement to make and although some other hon. gentlemen also desire to offer some observations, we thought that it would be possible to get through with these estimates in one day if we started early.
If it will oblige any hon. members, while it causes a great deal of inconvenience to myself, I will agree that the militia estimates shall be taken up.

The hon. Minister of Militia and Defence mentioned to me that he desired to make such an arrangement and I left him to arrange with the hon. Minister of Public Works. Very good: let it be understood that the Militia estimates will be taken up to-morrow.
Motion agreed to, and House adjourned at 11.30 p.m.
